speakeroldname: Mr. A. B. WARBURTON (Queens, P.E.I.) moved:
subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
For a copy of aU reports, correspondence end documents, not always brought down, including report of survey made in 1909 of the harbour of (Cape John and Tatamagouche bay, in the counties of Pictou and Colchester in the province of Nova Scotia, relating to the route of the winter steamers between Prince Edward Island and the mainland of Canada, and suggesting or recommending a change or changes on such route, and an increase in the number of trips daily of such winter steamers; also a copy of all similar papers, not already brought down, relating to the route of the summer mail steamers between Charlottetown and the mainland of Canada, and suggesting a change in that route, and an increase in the number of trips daily; and also with regard to connecting such suggested route with a point on the Intercolonial railway. Also for a copy of all such similar papers, if any, relating to or suggesting the route between Cape Traverse in Prince Edward Island and Cape Tormentine in the mainland, as a route for the winter and summer steamers. Also for a copy of all reports, papers and correspondence relating to additional or improved aids to navigation of the harbour of Charlottetown and entrance thereto and in Tatamagouche bay and harbour.
He said: In bringing this resolution before the House I desire to make a few remarks. On previous occasions I have brought this question before parliament. It may be wearisome to hon. members of this House to hear this matter brought up periodically, but there is no other way open to me to obtain the object I have in view. I must press upon the attention of the House the difficulties with which we have to contend in Prince Edward Island, and try to enlist the sympathy of the government and of the House in an effort to remove those difficulties. Last year I went, into this subject with considerable detail, pointing out the various routes which were possibly available for carrying on a winter service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I also went at considerable detail into the nature of the topography of the harbour on the Prince Edward Island side, that is the Charlottetown harbour, which I think is the best harbour on that side of the straits for the purpose of winter communication. I do not propose to go into that branch of the subject again this afternoon with the same detail that I did last year, but for the purpose of my argument it will be necessary for me to touch upon it. I wish to point out that the channel leading into Charlottetown, about five miles from where it leaves deep water in the Straits of Northumberland is a couple of miles wide, but it gradually narrows until it gets to the mouth of the harbour where it is a third of a mile wide. The depth of Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
water varies from 37 feet to 75 feet, a depth ample for any ship that floats. There is plenty of water there to prevent the ice from grounding and the ice never does ground. In addition to that, there are three rivers flowing into the Charlottetown harbour, which has an entrance of a quarter or third of a mile, and as the tide ebbs and flows twice a day, it creates very powerful currents. There is a current sweeping in and out of that harbour at that channel, which keeps it pretty free from ice. As I pointed out last year, for winter purposes, and also for summer purposes, owing to the larger ships that now come there in the summer time than formerly came, some improvements are required to aid navigation. In the winter, of course, the bell buoys have to be taken up, they cannot be left out: consequently vessels plying there in winter have no buoys to guide them in coming in or going out of the harbour. Most all of the time they can manage very well without these buoys, but if by any chance vessels require to come in at night, there might be some difficulty, although even at night it would not be so bad. But occasionally, as I pointed out last year, as the weather changes, as the weather gets colder than the water, or warmer than the water, the change in temperature causes a haze to rise sufficiently high above the water, on a fine day, to interfere with navigators seeing the lights on the land itself. It is a matter of rare occurrence, this year and last year it did not happen at all,"and it only occurs once in a while. But for all purposes, in the summer as well as in the winter, some improved aids to navigation are required. One that I suggested last year has been made, that is, the placing of a gun on St. Peter's island on the right hand side of the harbour, where one has now been established. In addition, the Board of Trade have been urging the erection of a light-house at the extreme outer or eastern end of St. Peter's island bar. I think there is a better place still. There is a bank or mound of sandstone at a considerable further distance out, almost at the edge of the channel coming into Charlottetown, upon which there are only nine feet of water and upon which a lighthouse if built, would answer all purposes. Probably the department would be able to abolish some of the lights there which are now to be found lighting the entrance of that harbour.
We had a water survey made I believe a year, or a year and a half ago, in the summer of 1909, of Tatamagouche bay on the Nova Scotia side, directly opposite Charlottetown. I may say that the distance from wharf to wharf, from the Charlottetown wharf and the wharf that could be built in deep water in Tatamagouche bay either on the Colchester side, or the Pictou side, would only be some 25 miles. I am in-

formed, and I think I can say with certainty, that the survey made there found a depth of 30 feet of water on the Cape John or Pictou side of that bay, and a depth of 27 feet on the Colchester side. Whichever side is chosen for a pier to connect with that line of railway, I am informed that a wharf not exceeding 1,200 feet in length would be ample in order to reach this deep water. I brought this matter of Tatamagouche bay up last year, and objection was taken by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that it would require an immense amount of dredging. I think my hon. friend had not taken the precaution to acquaint himself with the conditions of Tatamagouche bay, or he would scarcely have made that remark. But his statement uncontradicted is liable to create prejudice against this route. Now, the very fact that the water on one side of that bay is 27 feet in depth, and on the other side 30 feet, and that the channel from the mainland through the Straits is of not less a depth than that, is in itself a sufficient answer to anv objection that dredging would be required there. The winter steamers never require more than 20 feet of water, as they draw only 17J to 18 feet, so there would be a depth of some two feet more than would be required under any circumstances. I wish to emphasize the fact that dredging could not be required on account of the depth of water. I do so for the reason that persistent efforts have been made to prejudice and belittle this route by making out that such dredging would be required. A year ago the department very properly undertook to investigate the ice conditions in Tatamagouche bay, and in the winter of 1909-10, I believe that investigations were carried on there to see what those ice conditions were. It so happened that the winter of 1909-10 was an exceptionally mild one, there was very little ice, and I have no doubt that an investigation held under those conditions would not be as satisfactory as if it were held when there .was more ice. Almost every winter there was more ice than there was that year, there must be much more ice now, and I would like to have an investigation made under the worst conditions as well as under the best. The tides in the Straits of Northumberland at either end are very swift. They meet in the centre and when they ebb or flow they do so at a rate varying from three to four knots. It so happens that they practically meet in the neighbourhood of Tatamagouche bay, and at that particular part the tide' runs at a rate of half a knot which is almost still water.
When I took this matter up the year before last and last year I had to encounter the opposition-I do not blame him for it- of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). This question of winter navigation
has been brought up time and again, although I do not think that until I took it up in the first session of this parliament the route which I am now advocating and have advocated continuously had been seriously taken in hand. Other routes have been tested, but this has not been, and I wish to point out that, owing to the short distance across Tatamagouche bay, laying directly opposite Charlottetown, very much less time would be required in making the trip across there, and the difficulties which have arisen this winter, as they have arisen regularly, would not arise. Steamers running to and fro between Prince Edward Island and the mainland occasionally encounter a snow storm, or mist, just aftef leaving the harbour, and you cannot expect any vessel to pursue her way in the ice when there is a snowstorm. But the distance between Tatamagouche and Charlottetown harbour is so short-it is only 25 miles from Charlottetown wharf to the proposed wharf in Tatamagouche bay, and not more than 18 or 20 miles from land to land-that a ship, such as the ' Earl Grey,' leaving Charlottetown would be able to cross from shore to shore, from harbour to harbour, in an hour and a half or less; in fact, she would get inside the entrance to the harbour in an hour. Any captain with his eyes open could tell, before starting, if he had time to make the short run from harbour to harbour, and under these circumstances it would be possible to obviate any condition which would cause harm or danger. The objection raised last year, as in fact, every year, was that the members from Prince Edward Island are not agreed upon the course that should be taken in this matter. While the members from Prince Edward Island sometimes do not see eye to eye upon all questions, there are some matters upon which they dp see eye to eye. The hon. member for Pictou last year took this matter up and pointed out that he would like to see the members from Prince Edward Island agree on this question. At page 3192 of ' Hansard,' my hon. friend was good enough to say:
I have not heard the remarks of the hon. gentlemen who come from east of the island, but I venture the prediction that they will not agree with my hon. friend from Queens in the proposition that the present winter port should be changed and that a new and experimental route should be established between Charlottetown and Tatamagouche.
The hon. gentleman did not remain in his seat to hear the reply, but the hon. member from Kings, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Fraser), who represents the eastern end of Prince Edward Island, spoke upon that occasion, and he spoke very strongly, He said, as reported at page 3197 of ' Hansard ' of last year:

I will not say much as to the relative advantages ot' the different ports on the mainland, because I do not pretend to have as much knowledge of the Brule route as those gentlemen possess who have made a special study of this question. But I want to tell the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who I see is not in his seat, that if there is one thing upon which the people of Prince Edward Island are united, it is in the opinion that the Pictou harbour is the poorest harbour on the mainland for winter navigation. Let the government make no mistake on that point. The hon. member for Pictou almost taunted us to-night because we were not unanimous upon any route; but we are unanimous in the belief that the Pictou harbour offers the poorest harbour for winter navigation of any that can be mentioned. Let the government take that much fcr granted. Then I trust they will go on and make a good survey, and obtain sufficient knowledge to enable them to give us a better harbour. This is not my opinion only. I have studied the records and the reports of the surveyors that have been sent down by this govei'nment and by other governments, and 1 find there is a unanimous expression of opinion from these surveyors in their reports that Pictou harbour, on account of its shape and its situation, is certainly the least feasible on the mainland for winter navigation. It is a V-shaped harbour, opening towards the northeast, and without any protection whatever. When the northeast and easterly winds blow the ice into that harbour, the whole harbour is blocked with ice, and navigation is completely stopped.
Other members from Prince Edward Island agree upon that point. So that the objections raised to this change based upon the disagreement of Prince Edward Island members, or people, are not well taken, and there is a unanimity of opinion as to the undesirability of Pictou as a winter harbour. We all agree upon that point. I must say that although the hon. member for Kings does not hold the same political views that I do, when he took that ground he took a very manly ground, because he knew that he was, to some extent, antagonizing some of his warm political friends. I must say that I compliment .him for the courage and manliness displayed by him in expressing a view which I know he honestly and conscientiously held. But I have spoken upon this question on two previous occasions at some length, and the reply that I had from the hon. member for Pictou last year, in defence of Pictou harbour, was given us in a rather superior sort of way. He informed us that men living on the mainland had a practical knowledge of the conditions subsisting there, that we poor unsophisticated Prince Edward Islanders could not have a practical knowledge of the conditions, although we had crossed year after year, and that we could not know or speak about the actual conditions of the ice in the Straits of Northumberland. We have crossed and have been stuck in the straits time and time again, but he Mr. WARBURTON.
said that we cculd not know and speak about those conditions as could those living on the mainland, who never had crossed there at all. That seemed to be the inference to be drawn from his remarks. As a matter of fact, we, the people of Prince Edward Island, are compelled to have a practical knowledge of those conditions, because this matter of winter communication is one of the most vital questions which concern us. Any man living on Prince Edward Island who moves about at all, who does not know more about the conditions of ice to be encountered in crossing these straits than any man on the mainland must be a person of very weak intelligence. But while my hon. friend was talking about these conditions and about the superior knowledge of gentlemen living on the mainland, he, in that very same speech, showed conclusively that he himself did pot understand or know the conditions which frequently exist in the very harbour upon which he lives. I will show that. My hon. friend, replying to me and seeking to minimize the force of my argument, stated (' Hansard,' 1909-10, page 3192);
I am surprised that my hon. friend should onee more undertake to entertain the House about this imaginary ice bar that forms in front of the mouth of the Pictou harbour. I was born in the little town of Pictou and have lived there some 10 years. Only once in all the years during which communication has been maintained from that place with Prince Edward Island has an ice barrier existed there at the time of winter navigation. Since that accidental circumstance which occurred some years ago hon. gentlemen in discussing this auestion have talked about it as if it were a permanent and continuous obstruction that came as sure as the winter came. Any hon. gentleman who wants to make an argument for better facilities for Prince Edward Island, whether by increased facilities or a change of route, and who rests his argument upon the basis which has no existence in fact and which is an accidental circumstance which should not be used as the basis of any argument for a change in the conditions of affairs.
The statement made here is that only once in forty years has a vessel crossing from Prince Edward Island been held up by ice at Pictou harbour. I do not know what the experience of gentlemen on the mainland may be, hut I have a very practical and prolonged experience from which I can cite many instances of navigation being held up at Pictou harbour. In 1873, when I was returning from cojlege, I was stuck for four days in the ice off Pictou harbour, in a sailing ship, but of course a sailing ship could not be expected to get through when a reasonably strong steamer could, and I merely mention the incident merely as an illustration of my experience.
I can fairly claim to have as much knowledge of existing conditions there as any

man inside or outside of this House. Again, when I was returning from England in January, 1890, to run my first election, we were stuck in the ice off Pictou until the election was over, and any hon. member of this House who knows the anxiety there is about an election contest, will admit that I must have a very vivid recollection of that incident. But that is not ail. in 1898 I was stuck in Pictou harbour for ten days, when the 'Stanley,' a very good ship, was tied up at Pictou wharf and could not get through the ice barrier outside of the harbour. In 1905 I was detained at Pictou 14 solid days, and then I had to go round by the capes. I was home for a month, and in returning got as far as the ice barrier near Pictou island, when we had to disembark and traverse about two miles of intervening ice' to connectVith the ' Minto ' which came from Pictou harbour to meet us. That is the year my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) admits there was an accidental delay, but it is the kind of accident we don't want to occur more than once if we can help it. Again, two years ago, a member ol my own tamily in crossing to Pictou was stuck m tne ice lor tnree or four days and finally had to return to Georgetown. The year before that a triend of mine from Prince Edward Island left Georgetown on Monday and after trs'ing in vain for the balance of tne ween to get into Pictou, he got back to Georgetown on Saturday afternoon. This present season my brother was returning from here a fortnight ago and he left Montreal on Sunday expecting to be home on Wednesday, but he did not get there until Friday or Saturday morning, because the vessel was stuck on the Pictou side. Since then, the ' Earl Grey,' which is a magnificent vessel, has been stuck on the Pictou side for two or three days at a time. The ' Earl Grey' left Pictou on the 16th of this month m the morning, but she could not get iurtner than six miles from Pictou, and she had to give it up and returned to Pictou at half-past two in the afternoon. I have this in correspondence received to-day.
Cannot make crossing until wind changes: we want a good northwest wind to move the ice clear of the light at Pictou.
I am informed by letters received in this mail that the ice off Charlottetown harbour is not anything like so heavy or troublesome as it is off Cape Bear, which is on the eastern end of the straits, on Prince Edward side, nearly opposite Pictou, and where the ice gathers. The ice coming down from the north fills up the eastern end of the straits and it blocks at	Cape Bear, and
some other points further up. At the
present time, owing to the difficulty of crossing, our mails have to go round Dy the old Cape Tormentine-Cape Traverse route. I do not know that many members of this House have had to face an ice boat journey between the capes, but if so it is an experience they will not soon forget. I have been obliged to cross that way about a dozen times, the last time being five or six years ago, when we were eight and a half hours getting across. The crossing there is about eight miles wide, with about a mile of bord ice on either side and when you are trying to get over these hummocks of moving ice in a current running three or four miles an hour, with open holes_ all through the ice, into which the unsophisticated traveller is apt to fall, necessitating your travelling a distance of probably 20 miles to cover the eight miles actual distance, it will be realized what desperate work it is. I hope never to be compelled to cross that way again and nothing except sheer necessity will ever induce me to. I have here a picture post card bearing a photograph of these crossings, and if any hon. gentleman is curious he may have a look at it. I see here among the papers the following telegram from Halifax:
Halifax, Feb. 17.-Heavy ice has tied up ail navigation in Northumberland Straits anu on the north coast of Cape Breton. The government steamer ' Minto ' which left Georgetown on Monday, is still in the ice oft Cape Bear.
This is a week ago, and I think she is still in the ice, unless she got out on Saturday. ,
The government steamer ' Earl Grey ' which has made uninterrupted trips between Pictou and Prince Edward Island, was yesterday for the first time unable to get through the ,ice. She left Pictou as usual yesterday morning, hut was compelled to put hack on account of the heavy ice. She will make another at tempt as soon as possible.
There are, Mr. Speaker, some half dozen instances to my own knowledge of these steamers being tied up by the ice off Pictou harbour along the bar near Pictou, where the ice stretches from shore to shore, and where there is not sufficient depth of water for the steamers to get clear of it. If you meet with ice in the open sea with plenty of water on both sides and plenty of water underneath, a ship can smash through it because she has some place to dispose of it, but at the narrow entrance to the harbour where the ice is packed from shore to shore, nothing that you can build will go through it. I shall give a few more illustrations of the number of times ships have been stopped crossing over. I quoted these last year, and I am rather surprised that my hon. friend did not take any notice of them:

In the winter of 1898 I was stuck at Pietou ten days and was kept there by a northeast wind which blocked the place with ice. Many other stoppages have taken place. I looked up the other day in the reports of the department to see the record of a few more of these stoppages and I found that in 1898:
The steamer entered upon the winter mail service on the 23th December. It was not considered prudent to continue the 'Stanley' on the Charlottetown and Pietou route; the steamer, therefore, kept up communication be tween Georgetown and Pietou until the 22nd pf January, 1898, when the ship was hemmed in by heavy packed ice off Pietou island; in trying to get through between Pietou island and the ice jam the ship ran aground on the reef. After emptying the after-ballast tank the steamer was backed off without damage on the 23rd of January. The ice loosening up, the steamer returned to Georgetown, finding it impossible to get into Pietou. On the 21th January the steamer left for Pietou again, but could not get in. The passengers and mails were landed by ice boats. The mails were transferred to the Capes route on the 26th January. The steamer was jammed in the ice at Pietou from the 27th of January to the 2nd of February.
Again in 1901:
The winter service between Charlottetown and Pietou began on January 7, the 'Stanley' running in conjunction with the steamer ' Minto,' each boat making bi-weekly trips. On February 5, the 'Stanley' got caught in the ice off Pietou harbour and remained in the ice until February 20, and did not arrive at Georgetown until February 21.
Again, the same year:
Owing to the heavy ice in the harbour of Pietou between February 5 and 21, and also on account of the shoal water on the bar the steamer was unable to move out of Pietou harbour until February 19. This matter was made more serious by the fact that the steamer ' Stanley' was at the same time icebound six miles out of Pietou harbour.
Again, in 1902:
The service between the two latter places was begun on January 10. The service was fairly regular until February 12, when the 'Minto' was caught in heavy ice off the end of Pietou island and remained fast until February 15. She was then able to get into Georgetown.
In 1905:
In leaving Georgetown on January 25, 1905, the ice was found to be very heavy and the 'Stanley' returned to Georgetown, and although repeated attempts \yere made to force the steamer through the ice, it was found impossible to cross to Pietou until March 3, when the 'Stanley' forced ber way to the Pietou ice harrier, and the passengers and mails were transferred over the barrier to the steamer ' Minto ' two miles away The Stanley reached Pietou harbour. ' was found impossible to make another crossing until March 16, when the ice barrier, off Pietou, was reached and the cargo transferred to the ' Minto.' On March 21. the ' Stanley' then returned to Georgetown. It
I know about that because I was there.
On February 25, 1907, on a trip from Georgetown the 'Minto' was caught by a heavy ice-jam, in a strong gale and thick snow storm, and did not reach Pietou until March 2 and Mr. WARBDRTON.
from that date until March 19 it was found impossible to reach Georgetown again, although several attempts were made. The return trip to Pietou was accomplished only on March 26.
I think this pretty effectually disposes of the idea that only once have these boats been prevented crossing by, ice in Pietou harbour.
Mr, BRODEUR. Will my hon. friend be kind enough to tell us whether, from the reports he has received, the winter of the present year is considered as severe as those of the years he has just mentioned?

subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
The private reports I have received are that the winter this year is quite as severe as those of other years. But the severity of the winter is not the trouble %o much as the northeast wind, which drives the ice into Pietou harbour. It is not the local ice that is the trouble; but there is a clean sweep of 250 miles from the Strait of Belle Isle to the mouth of Pietou harbour, and when a northeast wind prevails for a fortnight, it fills Pietou harbour with ice not only from side to side, but right to the bottom, and there is not a vessel built that could then go in or out of that harbour. The Strait of Northumberland separating Prince Edward Island from the mainland is a narrow strait 140 miles long. At the eastern end the strait opens up into a very broad gulf something of the shape of a letter V. At the inner end of this gulf there is Pietou harbour and Pietou island. On the Prince Edward Island side there is Cape Bear. From that point westward the strait gets narrow. Further up on the Prince Edward Island side there is Point Prim, running three or four miles out into the strait like a wedge. The trend of the current in the strait is from west to east, and if there were no northeast wind driving the northern ice into the gulf at the eastern end of the strait, the current would tend to loosen up the local ice; but if the northeast wind continues for any length of time, the ice is driven further up between Bear Point and Point Prim, and there the steamers often have trouble in attempting to carry on winter navigation between Charlottetown and Pietou, or between Georgetown and Pietou. The ice does not pass Point Prim, which is eight or ten miles to the eastward of the entrance of Charlottetown harbour. The route I advocate is entirely to the west of Point Prim and is actually protected by it. In this connection 1 wish to read a short extract from a letter written by the late Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Mr. Des-barats, in reply to a letter of August 7, 1909, from Mr. Patton, president of the Charlottetown Board of Trade:

I may say that it is not the fault of the captains of either the 'Stanley' or the 'Minto' that the steamers do not come to Charlottetown; it is because it is impossible for the ships to make their way through the heavy, closely-packed ice in the strait, up to Point Prim, even with such power as can be obtained from their engines. Could either of them get to the northward (westward) of Point Prim there would probably not be so much difficulty in Hillsborough bay or Charlottetown harbour.
That accords with all our experience. The difficulties in the route between Charlottetown and the mainland do not arise to the west of Point Prim, but always eash ward of it. So when I am accused of basing my argument upon an Isolated case or an accidental circumstance, my answer is that the dozen cases or more which I am able to give, in which the steamers have' been hung up, bear me out in my contention. I can quite understand how an hon. member who lives on the mainland and has probably never crossed in these steamers in his life, can contemplate our difficulties with great serenity. If I lived on the mainland, and did not make use of these boats, I am not quite sure that I would feel so impressed with the necessity of a change as I do now.
My hon. friend, who no doubt, will dispute my statement, lives in a very nice place, on the mainland, where he has no difficulties to contend with, so far as the ice in the straits is concerned. But the people I represent, have to face any amount of difficulty coming from and going to the island. It is easy to say there is no danger, when you are not suffering yourself. We are told by the great poet of the epicurean philosophy that it is pleasant to recline on the summit of some lofty headland overlooking the .storm tossed ocean, and from that place of security look out on the ships struggling in the grasp of the raging ocean. Not because we rejoice in the perils and trials that beset our fellow mortals as they battle for life and safety with the angry waves, but because we rejoice that we, ourselves, are free from such trials and difficulties; and I think the old poet pretty accurately summed up the position taken by gentlemen on the mainland, who object to any change. I wish to make another statement, because I propose, when dealing with this matter, to deal with it as completely and as earnestly as I can. Another drawback of the route to Pictou is this, that the department is practically forced to take an inferior quality of steam coal. For this I cannot blame the present or any other government, because the department cannot very well avoid doing so, so long as the steamers have to come to this port. In this connection, I would quote a clipping from the * Guardian ' of the 27th of January last, and I may add that this is not a paper which supports this government;
A considerable source of trouble on the ' Earl Grey ' recently has been a poor supply of coal. The grade used is of such quality as to make it difficult to get up steam and to keep it regular.
Four weeks ago from last Friday, I am informed that the ' Earl Grey ' was stuck in less than a foot of ice. But if that steamer were able to get up sufficient steam, she is capable of making her way through 18 inches of green harbour ice. She stuck however, in a foot of ice, and the reason was that, with the class of coal she had on board, she could not get up sufficient steam. I speak, of course, of the quality of that coal, only in connection with the purpose for which it is supplied in this navigation. The summer steam boat people, who run their summer steamers between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, will not use it, but get coal from some other mine in Sydney which is better suited for steam producing purposes. So long, however, as this winter port in question is the one used, so long will the department be compelled to use this inferior coal. But any one can see that the winter service is not thereby given a fair chance, nor is the magnificent steamer the ' Earl Grey ', which cost this country some $500,000 or $600,000, given a fair show, when she has to face the difficulties of this winter passage with an inferior coal which only enables her to get up about two-thirds of her power.
We are told that the coast at Tatama-gouche bay will be very great, that it will probably cost a million or more to put up the requisite piers, warehouses, &c. Well, I cannot see any ground for that assertion. It would, of course, cost something to build a line of railway to that port, but that line will be built some of these days in any case. But to say that it will cost a million dollars, or even a quarter of a million dollars, to build a pier or such warehouse accommodation as will be required, is absurd. We have on .the the Georgetown side, a good pier and warehouse and ample provision for this trade when the crossings axe regular. We have at Pictou, an enormous warehouse which must have cost an immense amount of money, and which could only have been built of its present dimensions, because it was known that when the ice conditions in Pictou harbour would prevent the regular transportation of commodities, these goods would have to be stored at Pictou. When I was ice bound in the winter of 1905, there were five or six hundred car-loads of freight bound for Prince Edward Island tied up, and the only reason for the building of this laTge warehouse was, because occasions had arisen, and which, no doubt

would again arise, when, owing to the stoppage of traffic through ice conditions, it was necessary to have ample accommodation for the storage,., of goods which would otherwise perish. But there would be no such need in a harbour whose navigation could be kept up reasonably well. I would not at all be disposed to criticise if a -steamer were held up by a storm or .a fog as that might happen anywhere. We have not many fogs down there, but we have snow storms just as you have up here. But to say that this work at Tatamagouche, to make it a suitable harbour, would cost $1,000,000, is very much exaggerated. I do not believe it would cost one quarter of that, because you would only have a 1,200 foot pier to build, and a small warehouse. But even supposing it did cost the amount estimated, we must not forget that Prince Edward Island was allowed damages to the extent of $1,000,000 up to 1901, through the failure to keep up winter navigation, and that failure occurred during many years, when this navigation was purely experimental and it could not be expecte-1 that the authorities would know the drawbacks inseparable to this route. But these difficulties and drawbacks are now known. The traffic both passenger and freight, has largely_ increased and would increase still more, if _we were sure of continuous -navigation without any unreasonable interruption. And if these delays caused the loss of a million dollars in 1901, when the business had not very largely developed, what would the damages amount to since ? In fact it would seem to me that to-day we would be entitled to ask for aggravated damages, because experience has stbown that this port of Pictou is an impossible one.
I said a moment ago that our difficulties were due to the northeast wind, driving in the northern ice, and that the trend of the current carries the ice out of the straits from west to east and and not from east to west. My reason for this statement is this, that the steamer ' Stanley ' some years ago lost her propeller blades up in the Straits of Northumberland. She was in the ice a considerable time, and slowly drifted eastward some 140 to 150 miles. She must have drifted 130 miles to the east. In the old days of wooden ships occasionally a ship leaving harbour late in the autumn got -caught in the ice in the Straits of Northumberland and invariably drifted to the eastward, showing that the trend of the current is in that direction. Thus if there were no wind the natural trend of the current would have the effect of loosening up the ice even in the eastern end of the straits but, in view of the fact that this northern ice does not come down the straits beyond Point Prim, we have not even that to con-Mr. WARBURTON.
tend with. We have, it is true, heavy ice going up and down the straits between the two shores, but it is not that terrible ice which is packed in, and the distance is only a short one. From investigations made over a number of years, I do not know that any investigation was made this year although I have had a report, it would appear that there is no ice jam that would prevent the vessel from crossing. The western ice does not come down, it never finds its way up the straits except in small quantities; it is the ice that forms and piles up along the straits to the south and which does not present insuperable difficulties in crossing. In the early part of this season, up to the middle of January, the ' Earl Grey ' made trips to Charlottetown and Pic-t-ou. Up to that date we had a mild season. 'I crossed on the 14th and a sail boat could have crossed that day, but the weather changed the following day, and the next week they had it bad, a heavy snow storm set in, and the ' Earl Grey ' had to go to Georgetown. I have taken an extract from the ' Guardian ' of January 19, in which it says;
The severe weather of the last three or four days has evidently made heavy ice in the straits. Yesterday at nine-thirty a.m. the 'Earl Grey,' en route to this port from Pictou, encountered very heavy ice off White Sands

White Sands is between Point Prim and Cape Bear.

and was compelled to back up three times
to make headway through it. She came around the east end of Pictou island, making her trip one half an hour longer. A Marconi received here from the 'Grey' at 11.15 stated: 'Tlie strait is full of ice from Pictou, west, which is very heavy in places. 'Grey' in good trim, is doing splendid work.' At eleven ten she was abeam Point Prim and at 12.30 docked here.
It took her an hour and twenty minutes to come from Point Prim. The distance must be fourteen miles, which shows that she could not have had very heavy ice there, whatever she may have had east of Point Prim.
When she docked at this port, Captain Brown was tendered three hearty cheers and a tiger in appreciation of his successful determination to reach this port.
She went over to Georgetown. She decided for another reason not to discharge her cargo, and the following day she went to Pictou and brought her cargo up to Charlottetown on January 17. After that the heavy ice drifted into the eastern end of the straits and prevented her getting further down the straits. It was not the difficulties to the west of Point Prim, but the ice packed east of Point Prim that caused the trouble. In all of these cases, if my information is correct, notwithstand-

ing the severe frost we have had this winter there would have been very little difficulty, no difficulty for the ' Earl Grey,' in passing backwards and forwards in a direct line between Charlottetown and Tatama-gouche. If that is the case, considering the experience we have had in so many years, the proof we have had that Pictou is not adapted to be a winter port, the Tatama-gouche route ought at least to be tried, and 1 would suggest that even this winter, now that the mails are being carried round by the capes, and if you have a northeast wind the- vessel might approach Charlottetown, it would be a very good idea to let her try for herself and see what she can [DOT]do with the ice between Charlottetown and Pictou in this very severe winter.
There are also some matters connected with the summer route, but they are not of such moment as those connected with the winter route because we can always get across in the summer, although we have to take a slightly round about way. 1 have pointed out on other occasions that if we have to do business for instance in Halifax, the capital of Nova Scotia, it takes us three days to go a distance of 120 miles as the crow flies, about 170 or 180'by the route we have to take and return. There is 54 miles by water instead of 25, and we have to go over 100 miles further before we get to Halifax. We have to leave the island at 7 or 8 in the morning, and we get into Halifax about 8 in the evening, too late to do business. Then the train leaves Halifax at eight o'clock the next morning too early to " do business, ~so if you have any business to do you have to spend a third day in Halifax, and get back to the island somewhere about eight in the evening. I would like members of this House from other provinces to have similar *experiences for one week, when it would take them three days to go say from here to Toronto and back.' That would serve as an object lesson. There is no reason why we should not get to Halifax and back in 12 hours. I have been told that we have not the right system, but we should start from the island in the evening and come back in the morning. That might be very nice for those who did not need to go, but not for those who have to. Going in that way you would have to spend two nights, one going and one coming, in Pictou instead of in Halifax, because the way the time tables are arranged now, if you got to Pictou in the evening you would be too late to connect and to get to Halifax and vice versa on the return trip. It would be out of the frying pan into the fire.
There is another matter in which the Minister of Railways may be interested. The Canadian Pacific railway have acquired the Dominion Atlantic railway and the Midland railway down to Truro. They have
now practically a straight line from Yarmouth and Pictou down to Truro, and will have steamers running from Pictou and Yarmouth to St. John and Boston, in almost a straight line. They are now within almost 31 miles from Tatamagouche at Truro. It is inconceivable that a company conducted on the business principles of the Canadian Pacific railway will stay at Truro when by running a few miles further, by building a wharf and putting on vessels of 18 knots, like the ' Prince Rupert ' now running on the Bay of Fundy, they can make one or two trips a day across that narrow strait, one vessel between Tatamagouche bay and Charlottetown tapping the centre and east of the island and the other between Tatamagouche bay and Summer-side taking in the western trade. It is inconceivable that the Canadian Pacific railway having got that far will stop there for the sake of 35 miles of railway. That will mean that practically the whole business of Prince Edward Island will be diverted from the Intercolonial railway, the government railway, to the Canadian Pacific railway. That will mean a serious loss to the Intercolonial railway, as Prince Edward Island, instead of being a valuable feeder to the Intercolonial railway, will become largely a feeder to the Canadian Pacific railway. We discussed some time ago the question of taking over branch lines, and we should consider whether it would be wise to let the Canadian Pacific railway get ahead of us, and put this branch line down there and take over all this traffic, which they undoubtedly will. I do not think my; self it is in the interest of the government railway to allow this to take place, but it is going to take place. As I have said, the Canadian Pacific railway have these fast vessels, which will be on their hands, and they might just as well send them there as anywhere else, and they will send them there. When that happens, the traffic through Pictou will die of itself, and largely the traffic between Summerside and Point Du ChSne will also die out, although a larger percentage of it will remain there than on other parts of the island owing to the fact of its affording a shorter distance to the west.
There is another route which has been suggested often, and that is the Traverse-Tormentine route. I do not propose to say anything about that just now. Of course, it is a short route, but whether you could lay our piers on the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island sides and establish a regular service there, I am not in a position to say. Before I conclude I wish to mention another grievance which we suffer by our not being able to have a direct service in the winter time. Our merchants and business men have been complaining year in and year out that they

have to submit to three short hauls; instead of having two hauls, or two carriages, they have three. We cannot avoid two hauls, in as much as one has to be by water. But I think there is no need of having three. As it is, the winter traffic is carried down through Pictou, which makes one haul. It is then transferred to the winter steamers and carried over to Georgetown, another haul. Then it has to be carried some 40 odd miles to Charlottetown, a third haul. This third haul is very expensive; it takes the profit away from the business, and our merchants look upon it as a serious grievance and loss to their business; any business man must agree with me that it is so. If the system I have been urging on this House the last two or (Jhree years were adopted, and a route made directly across from Charlottetown to Tatamagouche these three short hauls would be obviated. While the route from Cape Traverse to Cape Tormentine appears to be the most direct, according to the map, and might be less unsatisfactory if it were made continuous, still, as we are at present, unless you build the tunnel, it -would not do a\yay with the three short hauls.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak at so great a length, but I wished to bring before you the salient points of this subject, and to point out -what our experience has taught us, and has taught others, who are not compelled to undergo the difficulties we have had to contend with. I wish to commend this matter to the favourable consideration of the House, and to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who, I must say, has always displayed the most lively interest in this winter navigation, and has done much to improve it. I specially commend it to him, and to the government, and I hope that one of these days an effort will be made to remove this unnecessary disability.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. RICHARDS (Prince, Prince Edward Island).
subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
At the last session of this House I took occasion to make a few observations on this important question of transportation in the winter season between Prince Edward Island and the mainland of Canada, and this afternoon I propose to say something more on the same subject. It is very important to us on the island to have the best route that can possibly be selected for our winter service, though there is a considerable variety of opinion as to which route is Teally the best. As I said on a former occasion, if it -can be shown that the route between Charlottetown and Tatamagouche is the best route and that it can be kept open during the whole winter, then I should say that the people of the province -would be in favour of it. On the other hand, if it is not considered to be the most practicable route, and that the Georgetown-Pictou route is a better one, Mr. WARBDRTON.
then I would say that we should adopt the latter. But a question as to which is the best route can only be settled by investigations, and I do not see that there can be any objection to making further investigation, in fact, I think it would be a proper step to take. We have had this winter unusually severe weather, in fact, at the present time there is heavy ice around the coast of Prince Edward Island, and around the coast of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and steamers have been considerably delayed, though, on the whole, they have done remarkably good work. Trade over this winter transportation has grown very largely of recent years. A large quantity of produce of all kinds is taken over by these boats, and it is highly in the interest of the people of the province that we should have the most regular and convenient route that can be chosen. Now, I am not going to dwell at length upon this phase of the subject, because it has been so well discussed by my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton), who has just Tesumed his seat. But I rise this afternoon more especially to draw the attention of the House and of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the desirability of making proper arrangements at Srwnmer-side in the fall of the year by which one of the steamers could be sent to that place and take away the freight that accumulates there at the close of navigation. It is true that the ' Minto ' was sent there last fall. She made one trip, and it appears she loaded with a large cargo at Summerside. But instead, of landing it at Cape Tormentine, she went on to Pictou and discharged it there. This arrangement was not at all satisfactory to the people of that town, and of the county I represent, There was considerable annoyance and vexation caused in consequence of the boat not remaining on what is called the western route for a longer period than she [DOT] did. Where the blame lies I am not prepared to say, but I have been told that proper arrangements had not been made at Cape Tormentine by which the boat could land her freight there as should have been done, and for that reason the officers of the boat decided to proceed to Pictou. Now, if that statement is correct, I presume it was an oversight on the part of some one. I hope that when another winter comes round such arrangements will be made as will avoid any inconvenience to the handling of freight at the Cape Tormentine pier.
Summerside is one of the best harbours of the island. Some of the shoal places in that harbour have recently been dredged. Further dredging of the north shoal or middle ground is much needed and will, I hope, soon be attended to. During the summer months of each year large steamers, such as those of the Black Diamond Line and other boats, make that place a port

of call. There is a railway wharf with which the trains make connection. There is a fairly good warehouse on it, although in that regard some improvement is needed. The export trade, I may say is very large from that place. During the summer months something like nine-tenths of the freight shipped from Prince Edward Island goes through Summerside and nearly all the passenger travel. The distance from Summerside to Cape Tormentine is not more than 17 miles, so that the trip is made over there in a little more than an hour. Summerside is situated in the midst of a most thriving and prosperous farming community. It has several large business establishments, three at least of the stores being among the largest of the maritime provinces, the volume of business is very large and as our agricultural development goes on, and it is going on very rapidly, we will make great progress in that rfegard and the amount of stuff shipped from that port will increase to ten times what it was last year-perhaps a greater extent. Considering all these things I wish to draw the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) to the importance, when next fall comes around, of having such arrangements made as will give proper facilities for shipping freight after the summer steamers stop running. ' This is an important matter to my constituents, and it is an important matter to the' people who live in a part of Queens county represented by hon. friends who sit beside me. A great deal of the produce from their countv goes that way, _so that it is not a local matter alone, but it is one of provincial interest. I found the Minister of Marine and Fisheries very readv last year and on other occasions to do the best he could to meet the views of the people of my county and my own views in regard to transportation late in the fall of the year, but, unfortunately, last season things did not work at all in a satisfactory way and I would like to impress upon my hon. friend the great importance of having proper arrangements made in good time so that there will be no delay and no difficulty. I would also point out to him the desirability of giving instructions to the officers of the boats that they will not leave that port upon the first appearance of frost or because the weather may happen to be unfavourable for a day or two. They should have positive instructions to give that western route in the fall of the year a fair trial. The people have been asking for it for a great many years and until it has received a fair trial there will be grumbling and dissatisfaction. In my way of thinking, on every principle of right and reason, the people of that part of Prince Edward Island are entitled to have these transportation facilities which they have been for so many years demanding.
I had a letter only to-day from a friend in Prince Edward Island, a prominent citizen, and one of the leading merchants of Summerside. He has recently made a trip in the ' Earl Grey '. He tells me that he has read some of the criticism that has been passed upon that boat in an unfavourable way, but being a man who is well qualified to express an opinion upon such a matter, he says that the ' Earl Grey ' has simply done marvellous things this winter, that she is a fine boat in every respect and very much superior to the boats they have there-the ' Minto ' and ' Stanley.' There is, however, a feeling that the ' Minto having been there for a number of years, has now pretty well outlived her usefulness and people down there are looking forward to the time at no distant day, when perhaps the Department of Marine and Fisheries may see their way clear to give us another boat similar to the ' Earl Grey.' When we get a boat of that kind we will expect that the people of Prince county will have the ' Minto ' for service on the western route. But, as I stated here last session, we will never have regular and continuous communication in winter by the best of boats that can be built, because the ice conditions are such that when it packs in and around the coast of Prince Edward Island and the mainland there are periods, such as at the present time, when I believe no boat that could be built would be able to go through it. But until we get the tunnel we want to have the best possible arrangements we can have with regard to ice breakers so as to keep up communication from our little island to the mainland.
The day, no doubt will come when we shall have the tunnel, and I hope that day is not far distant. But, in the meantime, I do not think I would be asking too much of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries if I were to suggest to him that he might keep the matter in view of giving us a boat similar to the ' Earl Grey ' at no distant day. In view of the great development in our agricultural resources and of the rapid strides we are making in every way we expect that trade will go on increasing not only in summer, but in winter as well. From the favourable way that the minister has acted towards us in many respects we have every reason to hope and to believe that he will take up my suggestion with regard to a new boat and that he will give us the ' Minto ' for the western route. Then we would have communication from both ends of the province, this would give satisfaction to us and would remove many grounds of complaint that we have had in the past. I would again earnestly impress upon my hon. friend the desirability of giving instructions so that proper arrangements will be made next fall for putting a boat on the western route at the

close of navigation, or when the summer boats stop running, and that such arrangements be made and carried out in such a manner as will leave no cause for complaint.

speakeroldname: Mr. AUSTIN L. FRASER (Kings, Prince Edward Island).
subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is sometimes asked by members of this House, why the members from Prince Edward Island take up so much time- perhaps they may use the word ' valuable ' time-pressing their claims before this House, and discussing this matter of winter communication. The reason why we do this, is not far to seek. When our province entered confederation, one of the things that were promised at that time was that this government -would give us continuous and efficient steam communication with the mainland for the carriage of mails and passengers. I am sorry that neither this government nor the former government has been able to carry out this provision. I am safe in saying that until the last effort is made to fulfil this provision of the terms of confederation, the members of Trince Edward Island will be compelled to occupy more or less of the time of parliament in advocating their case, and that ii my excuse, if excuse be needed, for speaking now. The present winter has been a very severe one all over the North American continent, and in respect to the carriage of mails between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, we are to-day bringing them across in small iceboats between the capes, just as we did fifty years ago. No improvement therefore, has been made in this respect in half a century, when everything else around us has made a wonderful advance. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I have no knowledge of the feasibility of the new Tatamagouche route proposed by the mover of tljis motion (Mr. Warburton), and if parliament' or the country is in possession of any exact information concerning it, I have been unable to discover it. I do not wish to say anything against that route for I would be glad to see a new harbour on the mainland but, while not taking back anything I said last year about the difficulty of winter communication being at Pictou, I would say to the government: Before you abandon that route and take up a new route, you should feel perfectly convinced that the new route will be the solution of the difficulty. Unless the government has positive knowledge that the new Tatamagouche harbour will be a better harbour than Pictou harbour, it would be a waste of money to experiment on Tatamagouche. There is, in my own county, Georgetown harbour, which is without doubt, the best harbour on the island, and even if Tatamagouche should turn out favourably, the steamers would still have to come to Mr. RICHARDS.
Georgetown from Tatamagouche, because I believe it is impossible to navigate the Straits of Northumberland into Charlottetown harbour in heavy winter ice. I am informed, and I believe it to be true, because I have often entered Charlottetown harbour, that u is a siiallow harbour and one great danger is that, if the iceboat touches bottom, a catastrophe would happen, because the running ice would pile over the boat. Above all, what is required" by ice navigators, is plenty of water and plenty of sea room. On one thing I can congratulate the department, and that is, that a. few years ago, they decided to leave, to a large extent, the navigation of the straits-to the captains of the boats. I cannot agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton), that the captains ought to be restrain ed from leaving [DOT]Charlottetown or Summer-side or any other port, when it is thought there may be" danger. Nobody knows better than the captains whether there is danger or not, and the department was right when it decided to permit the captains to use their own judgment and to give them a free hand in this matter. I feel that the men in charge of these boats, will continue to give the very best satisfaction that men can give who are engaged in the most difficult navigation on the North American continent. I wish to add a few words of praise for the captains of these steamers. Caiptain Fin-layson, of the winter steamer ' Minto ' has bpen for 37 years engaged in the navigation of this difficult passage, and during all that time, he has never lost one life or one pound of freight.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
If there is any man in Canada to-day, who deserves reward for long and faithful service, it is Captain Finlayson,- who after 37 years in active service, still pursues with vigour, his arduous calling. I may add that Captain Brown, who is in charge of the ship ' Earl Grey is, I am informed and believe, also a very experienced and careful navigator. I do not think the department need have any fear of men of this class, whose judgment lias been tried and found not wanting on many an occasion. I trust the department will continue to allow the captains to go in and out of such harbours as they deem fit. I am aware also, Mr. Speaker, that the merchants of Charlottetown and Summerside wish to keep these boats on the run late in the fall, to carry away their freight. I have no fault to find with that, but I do believe the government would not be justified in taking any risks with the ships. The government is not bound to find boats to carry freight; their duty is to provide transportation for the mails and passengers and* the merchants of Summerside should not forget that there are merchants in George-

town and other parts of the island which have a right to be considered when it comes to carrying freight in the fall and spring. The merchants of Charlottetown require these boats to be kept there at considerable risk, and if they had their own way, they would probably keep them there all winter, even at the risk of being frozen in. The department is not supposed to run boats for the accommodation of Charlottetown merchants. The Charlottetown merchants sometimes scold these poor captains, who are trying to do their duty, and they keep tRe wires hot up to the department at Ottawa, with complaints, and even some of the newspaper- editors of Charlottetown so far forget, what we should all join in asking for, namely, continuous accommodation for mails and passengers, that they sometimes find a great deal of fault with the captains, when in their wisdom, and as the result of their experience, they deem it necessary to go to Georgetown. As I have said, the merchants in Charlottetown and Summerslde should not forget that there are merchants in other parts of the island; they should not forget that during nine months of the year the merchants in Georgetown, Montague, Murray Harbour, and other points, have not a word to say about the landing of freight at Summerside and Charlottetown, where the great bulk of the freight goes. But, these same gentlemen find fault, because for three or four months in the year, the ships go into Georgetown, which is the only natural winter harbour on the island. 'Now, I must draw the attention of the minister -to what is really only a small matter in connection with the port of Georgetown, and I am sure he will have the complaint rectified. I want to read an extract from the Island
Patriot,' the leading Liberal newspaper on the Island, of the 15th instant, to show the minister that even at the port of Georgetown, where all the shipping is going, the facilities are not as good as they should be:
There was a rumour that a telephone had been installed in the railway station in Georgetown. A shipper however tried to call the station up, and he found to his consternation that the rumour was unfounded. Yet this is the twentieth century when the old stage coach is no longer with us, and many other old things have passed away. Nevertheless certain antiquated services such as a deaf and dumb telephone at what is now the principal shipping station of the island are still with us. How long, oh how long, must the public endure such back woods methods.
This is a small matter, and I trust, now that the minister's attention is called to it, that he will see that a telephone is put into the station at Georgetown, which would cost only $20 or $25 a year. It is very annoying to shippers and travellers who want to learn whether the boat is in or when ,
it- is going out, to find that there is no telephone at this, the principal shipping port of the province, and that the nearest public telephone is at least a quarter of a mile distant. While on this subject I wish to call the attention of the minister to another matter, for which he may be able to provide a remedy. The Charlottetown 'Guardian,' of the 16th of February refers as follows to the crossing at the capes:-
To-day we are for a time back again to primitive conditions, the conditions of fifty years ago, with regard to our communications for mails, passengers and freight, to and from the mainland. Let us hope that it may not be for long, and let due credit be given to. Captain Taylor and Post Office Inspector Whear for the promptness with which the change was made w-hen the winter steamers proved unequal to their work.
The change is the fourth of the season so far. The winter service began with one steamer on the Summerside-Tormentine route, progressed with one steamer and then with both on the Charlottetown-Piotou route and later, first one and then both steamers on the Georgetown-Pictou route, until that route has become impassable. Now, as already stated, we are back to the Traverse-Tormentine route and the little ice-boats of fifty years ago.
This means that until the steamer service can be regularly resumed travel to and from this province will be mainly limited to a very few robust persons in the most active period of their life, whose business is urgent and who are willing to undergo the risks and hardships of the trip at the capes. Women, children, the aged, and infirm are practically debarred from coming to or leaving the province in that way.
This is, of course, beyond immediate remedy. But better ^things were promised us by the terms of our union with Canada, and by Sir John Macdonald and by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, many, many years ago. And in the meantime what has jjeen done or is now doing to prepare the way for better things? Little has been done and nothing is doing.
An obvious need is a better steamer to replace the ' Minto,' which never was a good ice boat and is now practically useless in any emergent ice conditions in the straits.
This was referred to by the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Richards), and I thoroughly endorse what he has said with regard to it. The most successful steamer on that route was the 'Stanley.' After some years the 'Minto' was built, but it did not quite come up to expectations. As a matter of fact, it is well known to everybody that the 'Minto' was not better, if she was as good as the 'Stanley.' But the new steamer, the 'Earl Grey,' which was put on a year ago, is proving to be superior to any of the steamers that preceded her, and it is thought now that until we get the tunnel, which I thoroughly believe is the only permanent solution of this question, we should get another new steamer of the type of the 'Earl Grey.' I would urge the department

to consider the advisability of so doing. It may perhaps be said that in asking for this we are asking too much,, but I think not. When the 'Stanley' was built a few years ago, the government said to us, we are giving you the 'Stanley,' but the 'Stanley' has been taken off the route last winter and this winter and has been put on service at other parts of the Dominion. Therefore I do not think we should be charged with the cost of the 'Stanley;' we should rather be credited with it, since the steamer has been taken away from us, and this is a reason why the government should now give us another steamer of the type of the ' Earl Grey. This extract from the Charlottetown 'Guardian' continues:-
Nothing short of another steamer as powerful as the ' Grey ' as a sister ship-a pair of ' Greys '-can meet the reasonable demand till we are altogether relieved of dependence upon steamers. There never can be an adequate winter service by steamers.
But for the present distress it seems reasonable to ask that the ' strap passengers ' who help to haul the government boats and mails should be given free passage in return for their labours, and that the few other passengers who are compelled by age or weakness to remain in the boats should he taken over at regular summer passenger rates. This is a reasonable proposition. On sea-going vessels the man who ' works his passage ' is not expected also to pay in money for his passage. Any ' strap passenger ' who crosses at the capes earns his passage twice over.
The ice-boat service at the capes is a government service. Passengers who cross there and utilize it are compelled to do so solely because the government has failed to maintain the stipulated continuous service by steam between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. For this reason it seems to the ' Guardian ' that passengers who assist in the arduous work of launching, working and hauling the boats should be allowed free passage.
And the rates heretofore charged, and which passengers to and from the island have been paying for thirty-eight years since confederation, are exorbitant. The charge of four dollars per passenger for_ a distance of seven miles is exorbitant. It is 57 cents per mile. And the charge of 28 cents per mile for a ' strap passenger ' who works his way is even more so.
From what we know and have heard of Hon. L. P. Brodeur, he is disposed to be just and fair, and is not unsympathetic towards our people in their winter disabilities and hardships. We, therefore, appeal to Mr. Brodeur, and to the government through him, to reduce or sweep away altogether the unreasonable charges upon passengers at the capes. This request has been made before by the ' Guardian ' and has not been heeded. It will be made again and again whenever the people are compelled to use this route in winter. We smcerely hope that this matter may be put right at an early day.
I shall not make any further comment on this, as the hon. minister is present, and I merely wished to place it before him Mr. FRASER.
for his consideration. It is not fair that these passengers, who have to cross the straits, and who have to get out and assist in hauling the boats, should be charged the exorbitant rate of 28 cents a mile for that service, especially as it is a government service.
* One of the great difficulties in travelling to and from Prince Edward Island in the fall and spring is the uncertainty of the route you have to take, and I would ask the minister to remove that difficulty by placing one of the winter boats on the Pictou and Georgetown route on the first day of December and let it remain there until the first of May, and not rove around from one route to the other, as is sometimes done. The people on the island would then know that there was a decided route on which they could always depend, and they could buy their tickets and know which route to take to go to the mainland. Then, if instead of taking the Pictou and Georgetown route, they preferred to take a chance and go by Summerside or Charlottetown, that would be their own choice. This uncertainty about routes is one of the great drawbacks of our winter traffic. When I was going home during the Christmas holidays and got down to St. John, I could pot find out whether I had to go to the island by Georgetown or Summerside, or Charlottetown, and there was nobody there to give me the information. I would, therefore, ask the hon. minister to carefully consider the suggestion of placing at least one winter boat just before the close of navigation, say the first of December, and keeping her on that certain settled route up to the first of May, when navigation opens again. Of course, the general impression among the people is that the steam navigation company want to keep the winter boats off all routes until the ice forms and navigation is closed, so that the company may get all the passenger and freight traffic up to the last minute. But the winter never comes on any settled day, and there wiil always be an uncertain time, a hiatus, between the summer and the winter travel, when the people do not know whether they should go by Georgetown, Summerside, or Charlottetown. But if you would put one of the steamers on the Georgetown and Pictou route and keep her there between the first of December and the first of May all that uncertainty and inconvenience would be removed.
