speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
As I represent a county which is interested in this resolution, I feel it my duty to say a few words in its behalf. Ever since I have had the honour of a seat in this House I have heard this question brought up from session to session, and previous to that period this question was also brought up, as I sea by ' Hansard,' every session. If my information be correct, that the time of the House is worth $21 per minute, we have already expended on this subject more than $3,000 this afternoon, and if the hon. the Minister of Finance would calculate the time given to this subject every year, he would find that the amount of money thus expended would go a long way towards meeting the interest, if not on a tunnel, at least on a new steamer. Reference has been made to Tatamagouehe, which is in the county I have the honour to represent. Well, last summer I had the pleasure of visiting that part of the county, and an old resident informed me that very little trouble had been experienced with the ice there during any winter. From that district to Truro, a little over 30 miles, the railway, which is in nrospect, would give the people of Prince Edward Island much better communication and would also furnish a shorter route from that locality to Truro and Halifax. I would, therefore, urge the Minister of Railways to take up the question of building this railway at once. If it were built, and the government put on a line of steamers from the mainland, we would have one rate from Prince Edward Island to points on the mainland, instead of three, as at present. So important was the building of this railway considered at one time that two local members pledged their seats that if it were not constructed at once they would walk across the floor of the House, but so far neither of them has done so. although one has gone to the Supreme Court. I must congratulate my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Warburton) on the able manner in 123
which he has presented his case. As he has said, if the Canadian Pacific railway should build that line, that would take away from the Intercolonial railway a considerable amount of business. I do not propose to say any more on this subject, further than to urge on the government the imperative and immediate necessity for better communication with Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext: We have had, particularly during the last few sessions, since my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Warburton) has had a seat in this House, this question of winter navigation discussed from a new standpoint. During the last parliament, and for some parliaments before that the hon. gentlemen from Prince Edward Island insisted that the government of Canada should enter upon the enterprise of the construction of a tunnel between Cape Tormentine and Cape Traverse. I well remember in the last parliament an hon. member who represented that province, every year entertained us with the most vigorous protestations that unless a tunnel was immediately constructed for the people of Prince Edward Island, so that they would have railway communication under the Straits of Northumberland, connecting their railway with the railways of western Canada, all kinds of dire consequences would follow to Prince Edward Island, and to the rest of the Dominion. The Department of Marine and Fisheries pursued the same policy, that had been adopted in the past, of seeking to obtain the best communication that could-be obtained by steam vessels, and as a result of the wise policy of the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the ice-breaker 'Earl Grey ' was procured. She has now been on the service for two years and I believe every gentleman who spoke here today and every gentleman from the maritime provinces who understands the situation will say, she has been a great success. But the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Warburton) does not appear to have been satisfied by the best possible means of communication that can be obtained by steamship; he has to find something else to growl about, and raise an agitation among his constituents and please a coterie of patronage hunters in his constituency. Therefore this House has had inflicted on it for two sessions this long imaginative story about having communication between a port in Prince Edward Island, which is never open in the winter even according to hon. gentlemen who live in that province. The hon. member for Kings (Mr. Fraser) has told us that Charlottetown is an impossible port in winter, but my hon. friend comes here and seeks to obtain a winter

subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext: That statement is not correct. I appeal to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, if I did not back up to the member for Prince county to the best of my ability, to get him to send the steamer to Summerside.

subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext: My hon. friend from Pictou misunderstood me. I do not think I stated that the hon. member for Queens had done anything to prevent us from getting our steamer in the western part.

subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
I did not attribute to the member for Prince any such statement and I did not say that the member for Queens had prevented the steamers or tried to prevent them from going to Summerside, but tne coterie fie represents nave been continuously asserting through the newspapers, and otherwise, that the proper place to run from was Charlottetown and not Summerside. That was the point I was making, and had a right to make. The member for Kings (Mr. Fraser) comes along and tells us that the Hon. member for Queens did not know what they were

talking about when they spake of Charlottetown being a possible winter port. There is only one winter port in Prince Edward Island, and that is Georgetown, and I agree in that statement. Every man who has lived along the Straits of Northumberland and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, every layman, and every man accustomed to the sea, and acquainted with seafaring conditions there in winter, will tell you that such a thing as navigation to Charlottetown continuously in winter is ridiculous, that no one would ever consider it as a matter of possibility. My hon. friend knows that the reason the 'Earl Grey' is not running to Charlottetown from Pictou to-day is not because she cannot get into Pictou but because she cannot get into Charlottetown, and he knows that the coterie he represents abused privately and publicly that honoured public servant Captain Finlayson, whose long service in connection with this winter route entitles him to admiration from every fair-minded man, because he took the ' Minto ' away from Charlottetown sooner than they thought she should have been taken.
Captain Finlayson, who entirely deserves the compliment paid him by the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Fraser), took away the ' Minto ' from Charlottetown merely because he could not get in there; as a prudent officer, he had to take her to the only port in Prince Edward Island, where navigation could be properly maintained in winter. I regret that I have to speak with some heat in regard to this matter. But my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton) both last" winter and this winter, has gone out of his way to attack the constituency I have the honour to represent, and to make statements which are without foundation. I regret that he finds his. case so weak that he must take the course of attacking everybody who happens to be associated with another route, and everything which is connected with the permanent conditions which have obtained for the last fifty years, until my hon. friend had this new idea. Now, let us examine the facts. First let us ask which is the best port in Prince Edward Island from which communication could be made. My hon. friend from Kings says it is Georgetown, and I say it is Georgetown. Nobody ever proposed seriously to take the chances of making the long windings which have to be followed from the time you leave Cape Bear unless you pass the lighthouse, and go up to Charlottetown, until my hon. friend himself put forward this view. I say my hon. friend will find it impossible to get from the captains of the winter boats a statement that Charlottetown is a port which can be navigated in winter, or if so why did Captain Brown and Captain Finlayson 123i
go elsewhere? Captain Brown cannot be charged with not being rnxious to do everything possible to u' ilize Charlottetown. Why did these g< ltlemen in the exercise of their judgment and having regard to the safety of thei boats, remove them from Charlottetown? Simply because they know they could not go there safely, and they did not wish to usk the government's property and the li res of the passengers in attempting to enter that harbour. Georgetown is situated on the eastern portion of the island and faces the Gulf of St. Lawrence ; and while difficulties which are to be found in winter navigation exist in that vicinity, yet I am in the judgment of every one in this House who is acquainted with the matter when I say that Georgetown is the only possible-port in Prince Edward Island with which winter communication can be maintained at all seasons of the year. My hon. friend tells us that Georgetown is not the best port but that Charlottetown is the best ; because if Georgetown is the best port in Prince Edward Island from which certain and continuous communications can be carried on from that island, then he must at once assent to the proposition that Georgetown must be the base of operations there. He has to satisfy the government that Charlottetown is a better place than Georgetown to start from, before he can ask the Department of Marine and Fisheries to take the steamer away from Georgetown. My hon. friend cannot do that, and he knows it ; it is not a matter for argument, because the results have shown it, and conditions exist there which contradict any proposition of that kind. In considering this question I think we can start from the fact as absolutely proven, that Georgetown is the one and only place in Prince Edward Island from which winter communication has been maintained in all seasons of the year. Now, winter communication has been maintained from Georgetown on the island with Pictou on the mainland, ever since there was any attempt by any government to solve this question. I say the onus is on my hon. friend, and upon the gentlemen who are behind him in this matter, to satisfy the minister, and the government with evidence on that point which shall be so clear that there can be no doubt -about it. The onus being against him, they should show that they have something better to offer than Georgetown and Pictou, before conditions are to be changed in any way. My hon. friend has not found a better port than Georgetown to start from, and he cannot start from Charlottetown and go to the mainland at all.
He says it is unfortunate that we have these three interruptions in the transportation of our freight, as if no person else in any other part of

Prince Edward Island was interested in this question; and, therefore, because certain goods are assigned to Charlottetown, you must try and carry the goods to Charlottetown, even though the boats cannot get in there. That is, in brief, my hon. friend's argument. In order to sustain that weak premise, he attacks the conditions which he says exist in the ports of the constituency I have the honour to represent. Last year my hon. friend went over this question at great length. I endeavoured to find out the truth oi some of his statements, and I applied for information to a man who knew. I wrote to the pilot of the ' Earl Grey,' a man who has been piloting on that service for the last ten years. I thought he would^ be able to tell us whether tny hon. friend's information was accurate or not, and this is what that gentleman wrote to me on February 15, last year :
Pictou, N.S., Feb. 15, 1910.
Dear Sir,

In a report of the speech of A. B. Warburton, Esq., M.P., made iu the House of Commons on the winter service between Pictou and Prince Edward Island and which appears in the ' Patriot ' of Charlottetown, there are many incongruities, contradictions and untruths, regarding the entrance of ice into Pictou harbour and also concerning the grounding, &c., of the ' Stanley.' I would therefore call your attention to the following facts:-
1. Regarding the ice from Belle Isle entering the harbour, I may say there is not any of that ice enters the strait, and hence cannot find entrance into Pictou harbour. All the ice we have to fight against here is made in Northumberland strait. Ice comes out of Egmont bay, Bay Yerte, and other places on and about Northumberland strait in sheets, and moves east all the time till it ' brings up ' against Cape Breton Island, where it begins to back and fill up the strait. The ice continues in this way until a southwest wind drives it out to sea, after having cleared the eastern route, Georgetown to Pictou and gives a good crossing.
Of course you know the prevailing wind during the winter is from west to northwest, then the wind comes southwest and clears Pictou it blocks Charlottetown.
Now the northeast wind which he claims blocks Pictou is worse for blocking Brule. There is nothing to prevent the ice from entering and blocking that place so that nothing could come out or enter that port. Whereas the ice brought by the northeast wind as regards Pictou is broken by Pictou island by means of the tides about there.
Regarding the time three years ago to which he refers when we were blocked in Pictou 59 days. The ice came in rvith a very high spring tide and grounded, when the wind shifted as by that time the tide had fallen and we grounded. That was the only time in all mv experience I have seen it do anything like that.
That is the occasion of which I spoke last year when I said that it was the only Mr. MACDONALD.
time in forty years when it had occurred. The pilot agrees that in his experience that statement is correct.
As regards the ' Stanley ' getting ashore he claims it was owing to the heavy northeast winds and ice. This was not the case. The facts were as follows: We made a mistake as to the tide. It should have been ebb according to the tables, and also to the regular tides, hut the tide was ebbing and we _ -were carried ashore. Captains Brown and Finlay-son could substantiate that statement regarding that occasion if it were required.
To prove the statement that the ice is made the way that I stated, i.e., makes in Northumberland strait and drifts down. Take the case of the ' Stanley ' which drifted awav from Sea Cow Head on January 12, and drifted down hack of Pictou island, further towards Arisdag and thence down to Cape George and Palmere island, and then hack to Pictou island where she was freed from the pan of ice. The foregoing shows very clearly there is very poor chances for Belie Isle ice to get into oi1r strait and as a consequence into Pictou. We went to relieve the ' Stanley ' in the ' Minto from Pictou with coal, &c., and_ she was then stuck five miles southeast of Pictou island.
Let me say to my hon. friend that when lie was speaking about occasions upon which he was stuck in the ice none of these ice barriers to which he referred were found in the vicinity of Pictou. Here is an illustration of what I said last year:
We got within two miles of her, and got into heavy ice and had to stop there, whereas if we had continued to Georgetown that day with passengers and mails we would have made the run from there iu two hours. What makes the passage from Pictou to Georgetown si clear is that the tides open it. As a usual rule it is open water from Cape Bear to Panmere Island with the wind off shore.
Another good example as to where the tides run is that one winter a buoy went adrift from West Cape and it took all winter to drift down to Port Hood.
Regarding the boats being stuck outside for a number of days the ice lams them so that a ship cannot get free until a change of wind.
All those incidents of which my hon. friend talked last session as if they had occurred in or about the harbour of Pictou occurred out in the Northumberland Straits.
The foregoing statements are facts and can be proven by myself from experience, and also by the captains and other pilots, while on the other hand the statements made by Mr. Warburton are simply from, hearsay.
This has been a very mild winter, or the ' Grey ' would not he running to Charlottetown as long as she has been running. I know .this from experience, not from hearsay. I hope the foregoing facts will he of use to you in presenting the Pictou side of the question for the consideration of the hon. Minister of Marine and the members of the House of Commons.

subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
When the House rose at six o'clock, I had demonstrated, I think, that Georgetown was the one available port in Prince Edward Island from which winter communication could be maintained. That being so, the question is as to the best place for the steamer to run to on the mainland in winter. It is manifestly absurd to suggest running from Georgetown to Brule because Pictou island intervenes, but it is still more absurd to suggest, as my hon. friend from Queens has done, that the steamers should ply between Charlottetown and Brule. The hon. gentleman from Anti-gonish (Mr. Chisholm) has argued that Cape George was the proper place for the steamers to run to from Georgetown, and while it has the merit of being the nearest point- on the mainland to Georgetown, it labours under the unfortunate difficulty that it is many miles distant from a railway. Surely my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Warburton) and the special coterie whom he represents would hardly be satisfied with a proposition that the steamer, starting from the best seaport on the island for winter service, should land its passengers at Cape George some 35 miles away from a railway. I understand that my hon. friend from Inverness is disposed to urge seriously that Port Hood in his county is a place with which winter communication might be maintained, but there my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Warburton) would run across the difficulty of meeting the ice from Belle Isle which has always been the terror of their dreams by night and their aspirations by day so far as winter service is concerned. The result is that these hon. gentlemen are forced to come to Pictou which their forefathers (who probably had as much judgment in this matter as they have) selected as the best place on the mainland and with which the subsidized boats which are owned and controlled by Prince Edward Island people have maintained connection uninterruptedly through all these years. It does seem to me that my hon. friends from the island in discussing this question could have freed the discussion from the peculiar elements which they have introduced into it this afternoon. I say that the attack made by the hon. gentleman from Queens (Mr. Warburton) in regard to the coal which is produced in my county was entirely gratuitous	and	unnecessary. It	was	notprompted by	proper motives; it was	entirely unjustifiable, and' the hon. gentleman was going far afield in looking for some argument in which to discuss the availability of a winter port on the mainland when he dragged that question in, without	any	knowledge on his	part,	andwithout	any	justification from	even	the
people whose mouthpiece he is here. He chose to tell us that the railway accommodation provided at Pictou was entirely provided on account of the winter communication, and were it not for that it never would have been provided. The hon. gentleman does not know anything about the subject when he spoke in that way. Let me tell him that the four towns in my county contribute to the Intercolonial in gross revenue three-quarters of a million dollars a year, and that is contributed entirely by business inherent in the county and is not dependent upon any of the imaginary conditions mentioned by the hon. gentleman. 1 resent the attack of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Warburton) on my constituency in the strongest possible way, and I reiterate, that the argument' he presented to the House is not based upon a desire to find a true solution of the best way to maintain winter communication with the island. On the contrary, the hon. gentleman is prompted by a coterie of patronage hunters in the county of Queens who do not represent the people in any degree whatever. The hon. gentleman says now that although Georgetown is the best place to start from, Georgetown should be eliminated and Charlottetown made the starting point, although the captains who are sympathetic to maintaining winter communication with Charlottetown if they could, have been obliged to abandon it solely on account of the difficulties of entering that port. Leaving the best port on the island, these gentlemen ask this House seriously to adopt the poorest port on the island for the maintenance of the winter service. Where do they want to go; for what do they ask the minister to disarrange the conditions of 50 years in regard to summer and winter transportation? They ask the minister to take a route which begins nowhere and fix the other end of it nowhere. That is their proposition. I have here a blue print showing the results of the examination and surveys made in Tatamagouche bay; this glorious harbour which my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton) has found in his imagination after so many years of mental worry. _ I find here a place called Brule wharf situated in Tatamagouche bay, and I find the depth of water at Brule point and Brule wharf as shown on this plan to be 3 feet and 4 feet within a radius of a quarter of a mile of the existing wharf. I go out half a mile further and I find the deepest water you can get is 13 feet, and the hon. gentleman would have to go nearly a mile out before he finds enough water to float either of these winter steamers. True, the nominal draught of the 'Earl Grey' is only 18 or 20 feet, but, when these vessels are engaged in the winter service and their bulkheads filled with water which is necessary in order to enable them to operate in the ice, their draught is increased to about 30

feet. It is quite evident that hundreds and hundreds of thousands of dollars would have to be spent in dredging before the steamer could ever reach this haven of theirs at Brule.

speechtext:
My attention was called to Brule, by the argument of the hon. gentleman from Queens, and it is that point I am dealing with. The hon. gentlemen who are interested in this question will find that Malagash, in Cumberland county there is available water and at Cape John or John river in my county there is available water to which these steamers could come. Although my hon. friends have been discussing this question a long time, and have been occupying a great deal of the time of this House upon it, they do not know yet to what place these boats would run. There is not enough Mr. MACDONALD.
water at Brule, and there are only two places where there is enough-Malagash in Cumberland county and Cape John in my own county. Before this House is asked seriously to consider a proposition to risk all the money which has been put into these expensive steamers, and the lives of the men and property carried by them, I would like to see some accommodation provided at a point on the mainland which the steamers could reach; and if my hon. friends have any practical appreciation of what they are asking for, I am willing if they are willing to join with me, to go with them and press upon the Minister of Public Works the importance of building a wharf at Cape John, and this I have already done. My hon. friend from Queens must know that all the conditions that he argues against as existing farther down the gulf exist in an equal degree between Charlottetown and Tatamagouche bay: The whole problem of winter navigation turns on the question of the steamers having sufficient sea room when they are in the ice shove to prevent them toppling over, and the merit of the present route lies in the fact that there is ample room for them to run out to sea in a northeasterly direction. My hon. friend knows that the proposition of a winter steamer running between Charlottetown and Brule, starting from one impossible point and going to another impossible point, means that at all times the steamer will be wedged in by the narrowest kind of waters, and in the event of a storm from any point of the compass, will be liable to be driven ashore because unable to make any deep water for safety. In former years I have regarded my hon. friend's proposition with some degree of amusement; I did not think he could present for the serious consideration of the minister such an impossible proposition as the one he put forward last year, and has put forward again to-day; but the manifest feeling with which my hon. friend has approached the subject, and the animus which has dominated his utterances, particularly with regard to my constituency, warrant me in saying that he has come to the point where _ he regards himself seriously in making the proposition. I have no doubt that the minister duly appreciates the feeling that animates my hon. friend in this matter. The intelligence which has always been displayed by the department in dealing with this subject of winter navigation is such that I am certain the minister will regard it as absolutely impossible to take these winter steamers away from the only point on the mainland where they can cope with the ice conditions, where they are in proximity to the deep water east of Pictou island, and to start them from an impossible point in Prince Edward Island to another impossible point in Nova Scotia. I

need not point out to the House the inconvenience that would result from bringing the steamers to a point where there are no means of communication and no accommodation in the shape of a wharf or otherwise. Until such facilities are provided, my hon. friend is merely wasting the time of this House in making the proposal he has made. I do not know that I need detain the House any greater length. My object was simply to resent the aspersions which my hon. friend from Queens cast on the facilities provided in my constituency. My hon. friend has told us about having been in Pictou waiting for the winter boats. Of course, he has. Usually, when my hon. friend is not talking about this winter communication from a narrow standpoint, he is the most genial of men, and the people whom I represent are glad to see him there; but when he was loafing around the hotel at Pictou waiting for the steamer, she was not at Pictou wharf, but was floating about in the ice.

I submit that my hon. friends have submitted an impossible proposition for the consideration of the minister and the House, and they realize that they have not all their colleagues from Prince Edward Island with them. The hon. member for Kings (Mr. Fraser) tells us that beyond all question Georgetown is the only place on the island from which the boat can start. It does seem to me, therefore, that until we have wharfs and other facilities at the only available point in the bay to which my hon. friends would have boats run-and I am willing to join with them in an effort to secure those facilities-their suggestion that boats should run to and from Charlottetown is absolutely impossible, as has been proved by the events of past years.

subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
After listening to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), I feel it my duty to stand up for Prince Edward Island as he does for Pictou. I have heard so much about Prince Edward Island this afternoon that I have almost forgotten that there was'any other place in the Dominion; and if we could only get the Prime Minister, the Finance Minister, and the other members of the cabinet to think so, in twelve months we would not be asking for anything, because they would give us everything we needed. I do not think there is
any need of the hon. member for Pictou getting so hot under the collar at what my iron, colleague (Mr. Warburton) said this afternoon. I do not blame the hon. meni-ber for Pictou, because of the deficiencies of Pictou harbour. We know that he is not to blame for that; it is due to nature, and I have no doubt that if my hon. friend could change Pictou harbour for the better, he would do it. In Prince Edward Island we have two good harbours, one at Charlottetown, and the other at Georgetown, but we have none on the mainland. The hon. member for Pictou said we do not know exactly where to run the boats to. That is correct, but we want to find out where to run them to, and that is why this question is brought up so often. We know that Pictou is an impossible harbour. I was once caught outside that harbour seven days and had to walk ashore seven miles and during that trip got into the water two or three times. I, however, got ashore safely because I had an oar that kept me afloat. You can see, therefore, that Pictou is not all the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) claims it is.
My hon. friend and colleague spoke about the coal. In that connection I might say that a few weeks ago I received a letter from an officer on board the ' Earl Grey,' complaining about the coal. They said they could not make the steamer go through more than 12 inches of ice, because of the inferior quality of the coal, whereas with good coal they could work through 18 inches. I am not prepared to say whether the coal is good or bad, but the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) should have the different kinds tried and see which would give the best results. The ' Earl Grey,' cost a lot of money, and the government should get the best they can out of her in return. The hon. member for Pictou (Air. Alacdonald) said that if we would ask Mr. Hyndman he would be able to tell us about the coal,, but Mr. Hyndman is agent for that coal and would be very unlikely to say anything but good about it.
My hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) said also, that we should stick to Pictou harbour, because that is the harbour we used 50 years ago. But the people of the island are not disposed to think that what was good enough 50 years ago is good enough at present. This is an age of progress, and we should try our best to bring the producer as close as possible to the consumer. In the winter they are a long way apart. At times in that season we cannot get anything off the island during two, three and four weeks at a time. I am willing to admit that the government have made an honest effort to do the best they could for the island. My hon. friend from Kings (Air. Fraser) says it is the same to-day

as it was 50 years ago. In that opinion I do not agree with him. We know that there has been very great improvement. First, we had the old steamer ' Albert,' which did very poor work. Then we had the ' Northern Lights,' which was an improvement, then the ' Stanley,' then the ' Minto,' which was an improvement, and finally the ' Earl Grey,' which is a very great improvement. And I have no doubt that the captain of the ' Earl Grey,' with the experience he has had, could suggest some further improvement, and if the government would purchase another vessel like the * Earl Grey,' only improved, the people of Prince Edward Island would be fairly well satisfied. Of course, I do not believe that any steamer can give perfect satisfaction, but improvements can be made with the present one, and the people would be well satisfied if we had another such steamer, with such improvements as the captain could suggest. No doubt the government could then find a place to utilize the ' Minto ' without any loss. I would suggest, therefore, to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) that he should, as soon as possible, procure another steamer, so that we might then have two as good as the ' Earl Grey.' The people of the island feel deeply their present condition, but, of course, this winter has been an exceptionally severe one, and the steamers, have had very hard work. We have had again to take to the iceboats at the capes to carry mails and passengers. Speaking of these iceboats, I may say that the men who handle them receive a very small pittance. They have to work like galley slaves; at each crossing they take their lives in their hands, and all they get is $2 a day. They should get, instead, $4 to $5 a day. Each passenger pays $2 for the privilege of working his way across the strait. That is not fair, and I would suggest that passengers who work their way across should not be charged anything, i know that if any member of the cabinet were to cross once and have to work his way he would be strongly of the same opinion.
A few years ago, on one occasion when I crossed, the thermometer was several degrees below zero. I had to go into the water up to my waist, and my pants were frozen so hard it wag impossible for me at the time to sit down. I then made up my mind I would not cross again in the ice boats, but, nevertheless, I have since crossed some 20 or 25 times. The second last time I made the passage I was completely played out, and 1 vowed that would be the last crossing I would make, but when I came back from England I found that the steamers were still tied up and I had again to use the boats.
I have no desire, Mr. Speaker, to take up any more of your time, but I want to Mr. PROWSE.
stand up for the people of Prince Edward Island. I am only sorry that we cannot get the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) to help us, which I think he ought in gratitude to do, because, if it were not for the island, there would be no Pictou at all. We are the people who supply Pictou with everything it gets, and yet the people of that county do not seem thankful. Of course, I understand that my hon. friend does not like to be rubbed up against the grain, and if all hon. members were able to do for their counties what he does for his our counties would be much better off. I was reminded quite lately that if I fought as hard for Queens county as my hon. friend for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has fought for his, we would have in my county better results, but while I have fought hard for my county, I do not manage to get as much as I could wish.

subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
I have no desire to take up the time of the House, but the circumstances Justify me, I think, in making some observations on the resolution before us. During the past five years which I have spent in this parliament, the sympathy of the House has been extended session after session to the people of Prince Edward Island, because of the conditions of their existence. There can be no doubt that the people of the island are subjected to great inconvenience and expense, and that at times the experience they have had to endure have been almost intolerable. The question is what is the best route to select. Sometimes when lawyers have a bad case they take to abusing the other side, and we have had an illustration of this on this occasion. We have had a good deal of abuse of Charlottetown harbour from the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and a strong condemnation of Pictou harbour from the senior member for Charlottetown (Mr. Warburton). Well, I think that the condemnation of Charlottetown was due to the fact that my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) felt he had no defence for the port of Pictou, and the condemnation of Pictou was provoked by the fact that my hon. friend from Charlottetown (Mr. Warburton) recognized that his port could not be defended as a winter port. I agree with what my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has said as to Charlottetown being an impossible harbour in the winter, and I agree, also, as to what my hon. friend from Charlottetown has said as to Pictou harbour being at certain times in the winter inaccessible for weeks and months. Some years ago there was no communication for two months, because of a blockade in the harbour of Pictou. On another occasion Prince Edward Island was isolated during 48 days, and there is scarcely a winter season when there is not

detention during a considerable length of time, all due to the fact that Pictou was not intended by nature to be a winter harbour. The ice blocks in there so that you have virtually an impenetrable wall which no steamer can cut. This is due to the situation of that harbour, and its funnel shape.
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said that the capes routes as it is called is out of the question. I agree with him. That Georgetown on the island is an excellent harbour is admitted by all. Two or three years ago some papers relating to that harbour were brought down to this House which I took occasion to examine carefully. They contained reports that showed beyond - doubt that Georgetown, in the winter, is always open and the reason is given. As my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has pointed out, Georgetown is on the eastern side of the island, and that harbour is exposed to the gulf, where there is a wide expanse of sea, and the ice kept loose and mobile, there is never any trouble getting through if - you have steamers which are strong enough. In Pictou the conditions are different when you go down opposite Charlottetown, because the ice is jammed in such a way that it is impossible to make either point. I could quote from the evidence of Mr. Chas. Duguid, naval architect of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and also from the reports of the late deputy minister of the department to show that what I say in this connection is correct.
I could also call attention to the report of Mr. Windham, an expert sent by the 'Board of Trade of Charlottetown and others who must be recognized as having expert knowledge more satisfactory than that of simple pilots whose opinions were quoted by the hon. member for Pictou to show that Pictou harbour is not a satisfactory one, and also that the capes route has been tried and proven to be a failure. As is mentioned in one of the reports, that route 

the capes route-was simply a political route and had to be abandoned. It being established that the only harbour you have on one side on which you could depend all winter is Georgetown, the next question is where is the best harbour on the mainland side? Pictou harbour is bad in winter, proved to be bad, and I venture to say that Tatamagouche bay is just as bad as Pictou. Of course we have not the evidence of this before us, but I have no doubt it will be shown by the evidence when it is obtained that the same conditions obtain at Tatamagouche as at Pictou. Then the question arises where is there a harbour? The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) referred to a harbour at Cape George, Ballen-tine Cove. That is an excellent harbour, open the whole year round, deep, with
plenty of sea room and always accessible. The reason why it is open during the winter season when Pictou is jammed with ice is the same as in the case of Georgetown, because it is exposed to the open gulf, you have the wide expanse, the ice does not jam and is movable.

speechtext: What constituency is that in?

speechtext:
In Anti-gonish. In this particular case, I am not speaking with a view to making political capital in my constituency. Other hon. gentlemen who have spoken might be charged with making appeals for their own constituencies, in order to strengthen themselves with their friends, but I. am speaking from a purely altruistic standpoint. My constituents are not seeking for this as their right. It is not for them to ask for it as a matter of right, it is for the people of the island to ask it. I am only pointing out how they can have this difficulty solved, with very little trouble. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) admitted the conditions in Ballentine Cove at Cape George. No one can dispute the facts. The department asked the lightkeeper at Cape George to observe the conditions during the past few seasons between Cape George and Georgetown, and a report is that at all times there was open water between Cape George and Georgetown. A few years ago a coal laden vessel left Hastings on the Straits of Canso, and went to Georgetown when the island boats could not get to Pictou because of the ice. The hon. member for Pictou mentioned the fact that these steamers were down quite a way from Pictou, and it was not because Pictou harbour was blocked that they were drifting. No, they were drifting while those on board waited in the hope that the wind would shift and the ice would then be driven out and ultimately they would get into Pictou harbour. But during that time they could land anywhere along the eastern Pictou shore or in Antigonish, which are opposite the eastern shore of Prince Edward Island, where there is a wide expanse of water. I know that on several occasions when the boats could not get into Pictou apd allowed themselves to drift down along the Antigonish shore the passengers were landed on the Antigonish shore and were driven across to Antigonish where they took the train. This has been quite a common occurrence, and if there was railway accommodation, then every time Pictou harbour was blocked they would go into Ballentine Cove or Arisaig or Georgeville, but these are not as good harbours as Ballentine Cove and, therefore, Ballentine Cove is the one I would recommend. It is about 18 miles from a railway now. Two years ago the late member for Kings county,

Prince Edward Island was coming across some time in April and when he came to pictou it was blocked. For three days they drifted down towards the Antigonish shore, and he said they could easily have landed anywhere along the Antigonish shore to Cape George.
The next question is a railway from Cape George to Antigonish, a distance of 18 miles. When we remember that proper steam communication between the island and the mainland was guaranteed by the terms of the agreement made between Prince Edward Island and the rest of Canada, that this country is pledged in this matter, the building of 18 miles of railway is but a small and unimportant matter for the people of the island to expect, and a railway there would be an immense benefit. Ballentine Cove is one of the busiest of places in summer. My hon. friend said that the only harbour from some place west of Pictou down to the Strait of Canso was Pictou. I differ from him. The best harbour and the only good harbour is Ballen-tine's Cove. In substantiation of that I could refer to the reports of engineers who have had occasion to report on Ballentine Cove, and I could produce other reports that Ballentine Cove is the best harbour along Northumberland straits. Five or six miles from Ballentine Cove which is a thriving fishing centre there are magnificent coal properties and shale from which coal oil and other products could be produced. 'The reports on the coal properties are most glowing, they have been examined by large capitalists in recent years, and there is every hope and prospect that they will be developed. There are also valuable iron properties near at Arisaig and Doctors' Brook. This will undoubtedly become one of the best mineral producing districts in the country. When that time comes, of course, the railway will be required so that the building of a railway from Ballentine Cove to Antigonish would be only a trifling matter, so far as expenses goes. The railway would pay from the start, and it would be the means of developing a rich country.
It may be said that this is a new route. It is not. It was brought to the attention of the House a quarter of a century ago. In 1874 the then member for Kings, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Sinclair) called attention to the unsatisfactory conditions that obtained at that time owing to the condition of Pictou harbour, and he directed attention to the fact that there was another route which he had no doubt would serve the purpose, that it would be open all winter, that is the route from Georgetown or Souris to Ballentine Cove. Two or three years afterwards the attention of the House was called to this route by the member for Antigonish and others. At a later date it was advocated by my predecessor1 Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
in this House. Since I have had the honour of a seat in parliament I have called attention to it on several occasions. I have also called the attention of the department to it, and they have been making tests and investigations. Last year the winter was very mild, so it was not favourable for the tests, but an officer of the department was sent down there, he reported from day to day, and his report was that there was open water all the time from Ballentine Cove'to Georgetown. I have no doubt there would be open water between Pictou and Charlottetown that year; but that year did not afford a proper test. I hope the test will continue for a number of years, and then we shall know which is the best winter route by which to maintain communication with the island.	-
I trust the members for the island will look into the route carefully, and I have no doubt they will then be unanimous in advocating the route. Until then, I can do no more than direct the attention of the House to its superiority over other routes and point to it as a solution of the difficulties that now exist so far as winter communication goes.
