speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND MAINLAND.
speechtext:
My hon. friend's mo-bon asks for the production of papers concerning the route between Tatamagouche bay and Charlottetown; at the same time he asks for an improvement in the service in the direction of increasing the number of trips, applying his remarks not only to the winter service, but also to the summer service. In TegaTd to the summer service, I do not know that there is much correspondence on this subject, because the summer service does not pertain to my department. The boats during the summer service are subsidized by the Department of Trade and Commerce, consequently whatever correspondence may exist in regard to that service, will be found in that department. As to the summer service, I do not think the question presents much difficulty. Some suggestions might be made, but generally speaking, I think the service is fairly satisfactory. I see however, that there is .some difficulty in re-

spect to the winter service performed by this department.
Now, when the province of Prince Edward Island was admitted into the confederation, it was agreed that the government of Canada should maintain a steam navigation service between the island and the mainland. This obligation has been fulfilled, perhaps not absolutely to the letter, perhaps the service has not been all that was desired or intended. But at the present time, at least, we have what I may call an absolutely daily service. In fact, last year, the two vessels we had on that route, the ' Stanley ' and the ' Earl Grey,' were able to cross daily, and this year the ' Earl Grey ' has been able to cross throughout the season with the exception of one day, if my information is correct. So in that regard, we may say that the obligation which was. undertaken by the government of Canada when Prince Edward Island entered the confederation, has been entirely carried out. We must not forget that for many years past a great deal has been done for the purpose of improving that service. Before the province entered confederation, communication with the mainland was made by iceboats tha is to say, a service that is- still resorted to when absolutely necessary, was maintained to carry the mails. But after the entrance of the island into the confederation the government acquired a vessel called the ' Northern Light,' for the purpose of making the service. Later on, we produced an ice-breaker, the ' Stanley,' about 1888; then we procured the - Min to,' in 18901900, and lastly we got the ' Earl Grey,' during the year 1908.
Now, Mr1. Speaker, there is no doubt that the service which is being maintained today is far more satisfactory than that which existed prior to confederation. I suppose nobody will undertake to deny that not only has the obligation entered into at confederation been maintained, but we have provided the best available vessels to carry out our obligation. Three or four years ago serious complaints were made to the department, and in the House, to the effect that the service performed by the
*	Stanley ' and the * Minto ' was far from being satisfactory. In one year, I remember, the two vessels were caught in the ice, and the service was suspended for a
- considerable length of time. The result was that a serious^ agitation was started to im prove the service, and we began to examine the question, and to ascertain whether it would not be better to put on a stronger ice-breaker than the ' Stanley ' and the
*	Minto ' which were then in service. I remember that in 1907, when I visited Europe, I brought with me Captain Brown, who is certainly a very capable officer, and a man whose advice in a matter of that
kind, was of great value. Captain Brown not only came to England with me, but we visited Germany together:	We were advised that there were in Germany some very good shipyards which turned out ice-breakers of a high class, which were used in the Baltic. We thought it advisable to visit Hamburg, in order to acquire all the information we could. The result of our visit showed that the best ice-breakers were not built in Germany, hut could be built in England. About the same time, we- called over from England, a naval architect, to study the situation on the spot, and also to give us advice as to the best class of ships we . could secure to perform that service. These things show you, Mr. Speaker, that we have taken all the necessary steps to obtain the best possible advice in regard to ships capable of maintaining that service. I am glad to say to-day that the expectations we had with regard to the 'Earl Grey ' have been absolutely fulfilled. I have now in my hand the report of last year, which, as I have already shown, demonstrates that during every day of last year-it is true that last winter it was rather mild-that vessel has been able to cross between the island and the mainland We have found this year, which has certainly been one of the worst years that we ever had, a year, I think, without many precedents, that the result has been absolutely satisfactory. The ' Minto ' which was the running mate of the ' Earl Grey ' was caught in the ice and was obliged to stop her trips, but the ' Earl Grey ' was able to cope with the situation all the time excepting, as I said, for just one day. On that day she could have crossed over but it was somewhat dangerous, and it was thought by the captain and by our agent at Charlottetown that it would probably be better that she should not attempt to cross. The great difficulty that exists with regard to crossing in these boats is the northeast wind. Northeast winds come through the strait and cause a blockade which almost prevents vessels from getting through at all I have here a list of the different days or. which this north or northeast wind was en countered during this season, and I am going to give the House the dates and temperatures. Hon. members will find that in spite of the low temperatures and gales which were prevailing on many days, this boat has been able to cross at all time3 with the exception of one day. The boat started on the 17th December. During the month of January she was able to cros3 over from Charlottetown to Pictou. On the 21st December there was a northeast wind and also on the following days; on the 21st December the temperature was 30 degrees above zero; 26th December 10 above zero; 31st December zero; 6th January 13 above; 7th January 13 above; 12th January 25 above; 16th January 4 above; 17th Janu-

ary 12 below; 18th January 12 below. For three consecutive days a northeast wind was prevailing, but during the whole ol that time the boat was making a trip every day. I have extracted the following statement from the report which I have received :
January 18.-The ice was very heavy; the boat had to back up three times. So far the straits are full of ice from Pictou west aud very heavy in places. ' Earl Grey ' in good trim and is doing splendid work.
On the 20th January.-Still northeast wind with 7 above zero; they met heavy ice on that day, too; Jan. 21, there was a northeast wind; 23rd, through heavy ice, 8 above; 25th, 15 above, heavy ice at Point. Prim; Feb. 4,
' Minto ' was caught in ice hut ' Grey ' passed through; Feb. 7, ice close packed and very hard fighting, 2 above; Feb. 8, 20 above; Feb. 18, the two boats started running.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think these temperatures show the difficulty of the situation, and also show that the ' Earl Grey ' has been running all the time, with the exception of one day. I understand the suggestion which has been made that we should try to get a sister ship to the ' Earl Grey ' and be better able in that way to have a continuous service. I do not know whether it would be advisable to build a new ship right away or not. I think, on the contrary, that we had better wait a little. We have gained a great deal of experience, and we are gaining experience in connection with that service. We have improved our service from the ' Stanley ' to the ' Minto ', and from the ' Minto 5 to the ' Earl Grey It is possible that we might still be able to improve the construction of the ' Earl Grey.' We are studying the question. We are continuing our inquiries in that respect, and it may be that a stronger ship even than the 'Earl Grey' can be constructed. Let us examine that point very carefully, and perhaps some day the government of Canada may find itself in a position to suggest the construction of even a stronger ship than the one now in existence. I think I have carried out the promise that I made some years ago that I would get a ship that Would be capable of performing this service continuouslv without any interruption.
We have been discussing to-day the question of changing the winter route. Many suggestions have been made:	I see that
my hon. friend from Prince, Prince Edward Island, (Mr. Richards), would have no objection to the establishment of a service between Cape Tormentine and Cape Traverse. We have also the suggestion that a service should be put on between Charlottetown and Brule. Some others are suggesting Georgetown and Pictou, and another member has been proposing a service from Georgetown to Cape George. That means that there is a great difference of opinion between the members of this House who have spoken about the route. I am not Mr. BRODEUR.
going to give my . views upon this question, though, having had to deal with this subject for many years, I might have a personal opinion upon the matter. But I may perhaps be permitted to lay before the House some facts, some statements or some reports which might be of interest to hon. members. We will discuss first the question of the Cape Tormentine-Cape Traverse route. This question has been before the department for a great many years. Many many years ago, statements were made to the effect that if trials were made on that route it would be found that the service could be very much improved. Trials have been made between Cape Tormentine and Cape Traverse, but the results do not seem to be very much in favour of the opening of the route. The reports on this subject iave been brought before parliament, and they can be consulted. In the last two years my hon. friend from Prince has brought the question before me on several occasions. He is still urging upon me that we should open that route and that we should have a vessel plying during the whole of the winter between Cape Tormentine, or Summerside, and Cape Traverse.
Although I have not been able to go as far as the hon. gentleman would wish, still I think the proposition I made last year meets with general approval among the people of his county. It was stated to me by my hon. friend that when the summer boats ceased operating between Pointe du Chene and Summerside a great quantity of freight was left lying on the wharf, and it had to be reshipped to Charlottetown or Georgetown and sent to Pictou. I endeavoured to come to the relief of the people of Summerside. and I wrote the following letter on the 26th November, 1909:
26th November, 1S09.
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of your letter of the 30th lilt., with respect to the winter service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
After a careful consideration of the representations which have been submitted to me, I have authorized an extension of this service, as follows:

1.	From the time the summer steamers go off the Summerside route, until the summer steamers cease running on the Charlottetown-Pictou route, the department will give (ice conditions permitting) a service from Summerside to Tormentine, if possible, and when not possible, then from Summerside to Pictou.	_
2.	After the date on which the summer steamers cease running on the Charlotte-town-Picton route, the department will continue the service on the Summerside route, until all the freight then in Summerside, or which, on or prior to said date, has been shipped, or billed in carload lots to Summer-side for transportation to the mainland, blit which has not yet reached Summerside, shall have been carried over to the mainland.

3.	The department will not undertake to carry any freight to the mainland, which shall have been billed or shipped, even in carload lots, to Summerside. later than the date on which the sximnier steamers cease running on the Charlottetown-Pictou route.
4.	In case of emergency, the department will if necessary, immediately withdraw the winter steamer on the Su'mmerside-Tormentine route, xvliether freight is at or on its way to Summerside for transportation to the mainland or not.
Instructions are being sent to the agent of the department at Charlottetown, to have the ' Minto ' prepared to give, a service in accordance with these conditions.
Yours very faithfully,
.	(Sg.) L. P. BRODEUR.
D. K. Currie, Esq.,
Secy. Board of Trade,
Summerside, P.E.I.
That arrangement, as I understand it, proved satisfactory last year, but, unfortunately, there was a hitch this year, 'j'he freight xvas taken from Summerside in accordance with the arrangement, but when it arrived at the mainland the wharf was not in a proper condition to unload the freight on it, and arrangements had not been made for its transit on the railway, which is owned by a private company. I am quite sure that next year these difficulties will be removed, and I assure the hon. gentlemen that it is the intention of the department to carry out to the letter the arrangement detailed in this letter of the 26th of November, 1909. My department has communicated with the Department of Public Works, asking them to take steps to see that the wharf will be in good con-clition next winter. I do not think it is altogether desirable that the boats should remain longer on the routes, as has been requested by some, because so long as the boats ply freight xvill be sent there, and in the end it will be necessary to send the steamers by the Georgetown and Pictou route, and the freight will have to be reshipped all the same and dissatisfaction ensue. I think the arrangement we have made ought to meet the legitimate wishes or the people living in that section. The question as to a winter route between Charlottetown and Brule was brought to our attention by the hon. members for Queens (Messrs. Warburton and Prowse). They have represented to us that the entrance to Charlottetown harbour xvas easy of navigation, and that Brule harbour, or Tatamagouche bay xvould furnish a desirable port on the mainland. Acting on the request of these hon gentlemen, we gaxTe instructions to the hydrographic sur-x'ey branch to make surveys of Tatama-gouebe bay. and as the chief question was not xvhether the bay was navigable or not. but xx'hether the ice conditions xvould not be as difficult as in Pictou harbour, Mr. Stexvart, the officer in charge of the bay, sent us the following interesting report:

In accordance xvith your instructions a survey in detail xvas made of the northeast shore of John bay, in Tatamagouche bay, between Cape John and the mouth of John river, for the purpose of ascertaining xvhether or not it xvould he feasible to construct wharfs off the shore and a branch line from the Intercolonial railway, in the vicinity of the village of River John, to one, or all of these wharfs.
The survey shows that there is very little water inside the bay more than 30 feet deep, and that the 18-foot contour line generally skirts the shore, examined at a distance of 700 feet from the points and about 1,400 feet from the heads of the bays between.
This 18-foot contour line is nearly straight, and the bottom betxveen the shore and it deepens very gradually, there being no sign of rock outcropping nor of reefs.
The bottom is nearly all mud outside of a narrow fringe of sand off the beach. This condition of affairs exists for a distance of two miles inside of Cape John.
The land inside the shore line is slightly hilly, but is nowhere higher than 50 feet above low water. The banks close to the beach are generally steep, about 20 feet higli, so that there would be no difficulty in constructing wharfs or a railway line to meet them.
In addition to this survey, instructions xvere issued to make an examination of the hay in the vicinity of Peninsula point, this being on the south shore about 7 miles northwest of River John village.
This examination shows that the 25-foot contour reaches to within one-quarter mile off Peninsula point at best; that the bottom is rocky, and that there is a rocky reef uncovering at low water situated about one-quarter of a mile northwest off Peninsula point.
Whilst a wharf built here would have a good foundation, there xvould require to be a considerable amount of expensive dredging to enable vessels to reach it. The 3Vfoot contour does not reach xvithin a mile of the point.
A blue print of the xvork done is attached.
WM. J. STEWART, Hydrog: apher.
January 16, 1911.
But. there are other matters to be considered in connection with this proposal. To make the change proposed would require a new branch railxvay, a spur line, some wharfs, and better accommodation than exists to-day. The port referred to is on the Oxford branch of the Intercolonial railway. On that branch, I understand, no large business is done and the passenger trains are very few. I am afraid that if the route of the steamers were changed, there would be required at the same time to be some very important changes made in the running of the passenger trains in that direction. We also instructed the superintendent of lights in Nova Scotia, Mr. P. C. Johnson, to make a report on this question of the conditions of the ice at Tatamagouche and Brule. In his report, which is dated December 10. 1909, Mr. Johnson says:

. 3916
Regarding my knowledge of the conditions at Tatamagouche and Brule harbours, the body of water known as Amet sound and at the entrance to Brule and Tatamagouche harbours freezes over generally about the latter part of January, and some winters it freezes right out to Amet island. They have often teamed material on the ice to Amet island, but some winters they cannot do this. After Amet Sound is frozen over there is teaming every winter from River John past Brule har-. hour to Tatamagouche, bushes being put into the ice to mark the track to prevent teams from going astray on the ice in snowstorms.
There are also trees staking off the road fiom River John to Cape John or nearly to the end of Cape John as far as Reef Point. I have driven myself over this ice as far as Tatamagouche many times.
Not satisfied with that, we thought it would be very important to have a man on the spot who would make a full inspection during the last winter, and Captain Robinson of the steamer ' Vigilant ' was instructed to go to River John and strfy there for some months to study the conditions of the ice. His report is here. I am not going to read it, because it is rather lengthy, but it will be laid on the table with the other papers. In the face of the difficulties which these various reports show, and in the face of the divergence of opinion which exists among members and others on this question, would it be advisable on our part to change the route? It is certainly not our intention at present to do so. We would require further information before we could take such a step. The situation at present is this. Immediately after the summer boats have ceased running from Charlottetown to Pictou, we have the two ice-breakers run between those two points as long as possible. It has been suggested that these vessels should start at a fixed time from Charlottetown to Pictou and at a fixed time from Georgetown to Pictou. I may say that I had that idea myself at one time-that it would be more satisfactory to the people of the island if they knew that at a certain date the vessels would be at Summerside or Charlottetown and on a certain date at Georgetown; but after having ascertained the views of the people on the island, I find that generally speaking they preferred that the vessels should continue to sail from Charlottetown to Pictou as long as possible, and only then be changed to the route from Georgetown to Pictou. In view of this general expression of views, I had of course to recede from the position I had taken because the people of the island were more conversant with its needs than I am, and I was very willing to submit my personal views to theirs.
My hon. friend from Kings (Mr. Fraser) says that the conditions under which Prince Edward Island came into confederation have not been carried out in the mat-Mr. BRODEUR.
ter of communication and that they are today where they were 50 years ago. I think that is going a little too far.

I do not think I said that. I said that the conditions to-day with respect to the carriage of mails, is just as it was 50 years ago. I did not say that some progress had not been made, but that, on account of the frequent storms and severity of the winters, the conditions so far, as regards the crossing in little iceboats, are the same as they were 50 years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: True, the iceboats have been in use a few days, but according to the report I have read to-night, the ' Earl Grey ' has been running all the time in spite of the severity of the winter, except one day, and consequently, I do not think that we are open to much blame. The criticism I refer to, was not made so much by my hon. friend as by the newspaper he read, and I submit it is a little outside the true note that should be struck in the circumstances. My hon. friend agrees with me in the decision I have taken that in the running of these boats, whether from. Charlottetown to Pictou or Georgetown to Pictou, or Cape Travers to Cape Tormen-tine, that should be left entirely to the discretion of the captain.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I made up my mind a few years ago that the captains should be the. men to decide. 'They are men of great experience, honesty and devotion to the service. There are no better men in the service of the country than Captain Brown and Captain Finlayson. They are both old officers, and I hope will remain much longer with us. Some criticise them, and say they are too cautious, but those men have been in the service many years, and during all that time, not one casualty has happened. That is the greatest record which could be made in circumstances so difficult for any navigator. I prefer to see these men cautious, than to be more risky and perhaps meet with some serious disaster.
My hon. friend called my attention to the -question of a telephone at Georgetown. This is the first information I have had on that matter. I have taken note of his representations, and will bring them to the attention of my officers and see whether a remedy can be affected.
My hon. friend called my attention to the government reducing the rates.
I meant the rates charged on the little iceboats between the capes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I thought my hon. friend was speaking of the rates on the boats. According to a statement I have in

my hand, since we have had that service tinder our control, the government has expended on it $1,313,334, and the revenue has only been $385,744, showing a net loss of $930,864, and that includes only the working expenses. It does not include the cost of construction. If we take the cost of construction of the four boats devoted to that service, the amount expended on them has been $870,915.
What four boats ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The ' Northern Light ', The ' Stanley ', The ' Minto ' and the ' Earl G-Tey.' I do not wish to detain the House any longer. I was very glad to hear what has been said to-day. Some very important statements have been made which will not fail to be taken into most serious consideration. I may say that the questions which have been discussed to-day will be considered by the department and we shall take all the necessary steps to give Prince Edward Island the best service possible.

I have listened with much pleasure to the remarks of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur). I have no desire to flatter my hon. friend at all, but I think that my colleagues _ from Prince Edward Island will agree with me that we never had a Minister of Marine and Fisheries-and we have had some very good ones-who has taken more active interest and shown greater sympathy with the difliculties which we have to contend against, than the present minister. Should he ever run short of a constituency, he would have a mighty good chance oh the island, because we believe he is in earnest, and doing his best. For that reason, I am always trying to impress these matters upon him, knowing as I do, that in him we have a sympathetic listener, who will do his best to remove any grievances under which we may suffer.
I was astounded at some of the remarks made by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). He told us that the trouble was not in the harbour of Pictou, but out side in the straits. But I never have said that the trouble lies in the harbour, because steamers can break the harbour ice, but where the trouble lies, is off the mouth of the harbour. If it is not, how comes it that the steamers are stuck inside the harbour from a day to two months at a time, not able to get out? That statement, which I have proved up to the hilt, is sufficient to show that the trouble is with Pictou harbour. My hoh. friend read a long pronouncement from the pilot of the * Earl Grey ' and he also referred to Mr. Hynd-man, who, he said, vrould take a very different view, regarding the coal. Well, Mr. Hyndman is, as has already been said, an agent for the company that supplies the coal, but he is a high minded gentleman, and I do not think he would declare | that that coal was of the best quality for i steam purposes. We can quite 'Understand however, why Mr. Hyndman was referred to. There is an old saying: Divide and conquer. If my hon. friend can create dis-sention among the people of Prince Edward Island, that will enable him to still further postpone the time when we can get clear of Pictou harbour. But the gentleman whose letter he read at great length, the pilot of the ' Earl Grey ', is himself also a resident of Pictou, and has been for years and has no desire whatever to go into any other port, if he can help it. He is a very good man, but it is not in his interests to go to any other port; and as to his opinion on the value of steam coal, I do not think it should carry very much weight. I would prefer an opinion from the engineers who use the coal and work the engines, and I would be glad if the hon. minister would have [DOT] the logs of the engineers brought down some of these days and see what power they get up, although that is not included in the resolution.
We are told that in February Pictou is the only place where the steamer can run.
I absolutely take issue with that. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) had to make up a case and how did he go about making it up? I said and I say now, that the harbour of Georgetown in Prince Edward Island is an excellent harbour, I never said anything else. In the winter when we have storms and east winds, if you have four days' northeast wind Pictou harbour becomes an impossible harbour. But because I admitted that Georgetown was a good harbour my hon. friend had to make up some premises on which to oppose the argument I was using and he said that because Georgetown harbour was a good harbour therefore Charlottetown is a bad harbour, and then it was easy to go further and say it was the worst harbour in Prince Edward Island. As a matter of fact my hon. friend does not know anything about any harbour in Prince Edward Island. He knows nothing of Charlottetown harbour.
I proved from the charts last year that the entrance to Charlottetown harbour at its shallcwest part is 37 feet in depth and within the harbour there is 75 feet of water. We could take all the water of Pictou harbour from the bottom of Charlottetown harbour and still have water enough to float those ships. My hon. friend says that if you go into Tatamagouche you have no conveniences and no wharf. I know that perfectly. One of the reasons why I bring this matter up is to try to get the conveniences there. I do not believe it would cost more to do so than to keep up the enormous erections you have in Pictou, the work would not require to be anything like as extensive.

He says we cannot get out of Charlottetown harbour to-day. 1 say you can get out of Charlottetown harbour to-day with the 'Earl Grey.' I am accused of taking up the time of the House with impossible proposals. I would like to know where the impossibility of my proposals has been tested. We have had the entrance to Charlottetown harbour tested and the ice bored year after year at the expense of the people there and it has been found in all those years that the ice has never formed in such thickness as to prevent the ' Earl Grey ' going there.	I have not the same personal
knowledge of the harbour at Tatama-gouche, but I believe there is no difficulty with ice, and that Tatamagouche is protected from all winds. The longest sweep of the wind they can get at Tatama-gouehe is from Prince Edward Island and it is guarded by Pictou island and different points up the straits, it is guarded in every direction, as any lion, member can see by consulting a chart. The gentleman who supplied information as to no northern ice coming in there was prepared to make up a case. I can quite understand the strong desire to make up a case, but the information I had was from men who had as good information as he had. The hon. gentleman speaks of Mr. Hyndman being the centre of information. Mr. Hyndman is a first-class hydrog'rapher of the British navy and spent years surveying this' part of the sea and many of the charts now in use were plotted with his own hand'. You cannot say that a man who holds that position is not capable of saying something of currents and the way the wind blows. I had that information from him that the northern ice came down with the northeast wind and if you look at the map you will see that it stands to reason it must come down. I have had the same information from seafaring men and the only information we have to the contrary is from the pilot of the 'Earl Grey,' who resides in Pictou and does not want to leave that port. If it is not the case why have we always been troubled in Pictou when there has been a day or two of continuous northeast wind? lie says we cannot get out of Charlottetown to-day. He probably means that we cannot get backwards and forwards from Pictou and that is about it. The reason is that when you get east of Point Prim you get into the ice that is drifting in. As Mr. Desbarats, the late Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, pointed out, if you once get past Point Prim you will have no difficulty about Charlottetown harbour and its entrance. I admit that if you try to go from Pictou to Charlottetown to-day you will hare trouble, but it will not be at the Charlottetown end, it will be at Pictou in the eastern end- of the straits. We all Mr. WAEBURTON.
know something of this in the island, because we are forced by our circumstances to become acquainted with the conditions.
The hon. gentleman says his reason for speaking warmly was to resent aspersions on Pictou. I do not propose to cast aspersions on Pictou, I have a great regard for Pictou, but the fact that the hon. member gets warm over Pictou or that I have a personal regard for it, is no reason why we should be compelled to stop in a port and have people and mails sent down to the capes and brought across on iceboats, and our business held up for anything of that kind. That is what has happened, notwithstanding the statement of my hon. friend. If they get a few days of northeast wind that will happen again.
The hon. member undertook to say where I was when I spoke about my own experience of being tied up at Pictou, he says I was not on the ship but on shore. In 1898 I did live up in .the hotel, but in 1905 the town of Pictou was so full of people trying to get over to the island that I went on board the ship and was there the whole 14 days and I saw the efforts that were made to get out. Any one who had eyes could see that it was an impossibility to get out of Pictou harbour. You could get out of the harbour, past the lighthouses but not out into the straits, you had three or four miles of solid ice through which no vessel could go. My hon. friend says I was having a good time in Pictou. I must give my Pictou friends credit for always trying to make it as pleasant as they can and I thank them for it but that does not affect the question we are discussing.
Because my hon. friend from Kings said that Georgetown is a good harbour, my hon. friend from Pictou takes that up to again force his contention that because Georgetown is a good harbour Charlottetown is necessarily a bad one. We have more than one good harbour in Prince Edward Island, we have more than there are on the corresponding section of the mainland. In Charlottetown harbour and Georgetown harbour you could float nearly all the ships of the British navy; they are splendid harbours, both of them. My non. friend from Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) spoke strongly saying that Georgetown was the only harbour in Prince Edward Island and Pictou was no harbour at all, and that we should therefore go over to Ballentine Cove. I do not suppose my hon. friend was serious about that. At the same time I shall not kick up much of a row if you can get a good harbour which you can enter all the time, even if it is Ballentine Cove but Georgetown would not be the Prince Edward Island harbour it would be Souris in Kings county where with a little work you would have " a harbour open all the year round.
My hon. friend says that evidence has

been obtained to show that Tatamagouche harbour would be impossible. My hon. friend spoke of the harbour of Brule. The harbour of Brule is a harbour inside the harbour, I believe there is a bar across the mouth. The place I spoke about lies in the outer harbour of Tatamagouche bay where you have plenty of water. Brule, of course, is a place difficult to reach. The hon. member for Pictou said that no one ever dreamed of going to Brule. I tell him that in summer the steamers plied to BrulA fifty years before they plied to Pictou, within my memory, and it was only because the railway was brought down to Pictou landing that they left Brule so as to get to the railway. In Charlottetown harbour, one hundred yards from the wharf, the water is 50 feet deep. The water at the wharf itself where the ' Earl Grey ' lies now is 26 feet in depth. In Pictou we have sufficient water for boats. They had to dredge a considerable cutting at the entrance to the harbour in order to get enough water. I believe originally they had 18 feet, now they have 24 feet, which compared with Charlottetown or Tatamagouche, seems rather shallow.
I regret that I was a few minutes late in coming in, but I have been informed that my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said that these boats at certain times draw thirty feet of water, and that there is only 17i feet of water a mile from the shore at Tatamagouche. These boats never drew thirty feet of water. Ordinarily the draught of those boats is 17| feet of'water. It is true that neither the ' Minto ' nor any other of those vessels ever drew thirty feet of water, no matter how it was trimmed, she never drew 22 feet of water. If she drew thirty feet of water, she could not get into Pictou harbour at all. Last year the ' Earl Grey ' went up and down between Charlottetown and Pictou backwards and forwards when	there	was no ice in	thestraits. Last year the * Earl Grey ' lost only two days,	but that was	more	onaccount of the	thick	weather	than	onaccount of ice.	Last	year was	not a year
to test a vessel at all ; this year being severe will afford a better test. .
Now, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries told us that when the * Earl Grey ' started out this year on the 17th of December she ran to the 16th of January, between Charlottetown and Pictou. That is perfectly right. I crossed in the ' Earl Grey ' myself from Charlottetown on the 14th of January when there was no ice or any tiling else to interfere with navigation. When I crossed over on the 14th of January you might have passed in a good sailing boat. It is true that the weather changed on the following day, but there was no ice at that time. I desire to thank the minister for the care with which he has investigated this matter, and I hope that he 124
will do whatever lies in his power in order to remedy the grievous condition of affairs under which we labour. I do not believe that the expenditure of a little money at Tatamagouche or anywhere else is going to stand in the way of removing this grievance, once the minister is convinced that it exists. More than that, I believe that the main reason why my hon. friend from Pictou argues so warmly upon this matter, is that he himself is beginning to see that sooner or later, and I think sooner than later, this route will have to be changed. He sees now that, with the conditions as they exist in the other harbours, it is almost certain that in the course of time when this great change is made we will have a good system, with a harbour in Prince Edward Island accessible throughout the winter, and a harbour on the mainland also accessible throughout the winter which now we have not.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. H. MILLER (South Grey) moved:
speechtext:
That, whereas it is stated that on Canadian, railroads last year one trainman in every 199 was killed and one in every 33 was injured, in the opinion of this House it is the duty of the government to cause to be made a most thorough investigation as to the facts and conditions, as a result of which some means may be devised for the better protection of railway employees, and of preventing so great a loss of life and so great and frequent accidental injury.
He said: When I read in a Canadian paper that on Canadian railroads last year one trainman in every 199 was killed, and one in every thirty-three was injured, the figures seemed to me startling. There are no men in Canada, I think, more worthy of our consideration, or whom the government ohght to try harder to assist and protect, so far as they can be assisted and protected, than the trainmen who run our railway trains. These men work very hard, they expose themselves to great dangers, they endure great hardships. After putting that resolution upon the Order Paper, I made a somewhat careful study of our Canadian legislation and of United States legislation having in view the protection of trainmen. I find the requirements of Canadian laws and of United States laws to be very -much the same. I will with your permission point out the similarities of the laws in the two countries, aid then point out the important difference?, and make two or three suggestions.
The United States Congress in 1892 passed an Act intituled * The Safety Appliance Act.' That has been since amended at different times. The Safety Appliance Act of the United States sets forth in detail



what brakes, ladders, couplers and other devices and apparatus shall be used on United States railway trains for the protection of employees. The Canadian Railway Act, section 264 provides that certain safety appliances therein defined shall be provided. Section 30 of the Canadian Railway Act provides that the Board of Railway Commissioners may order regulations, among other things, with respect to the rolling stock, apparatus, cattleguards, appliances, signals, methods, devices and structures to be used upon the railways so as to provide means for the due protection of employees of the company and of the public. Section 414 of our Railway Act stipulates that every train employee intoxicated while on duty shall be subject to a fine not exceeding $400, or imprisonment not exceeding five years. In both Canada and the United States, tne laws provide that railway companies shall give notice of all train accidents. In the United States this notice is to be given to tne Interstate Commerce Commission ; in Canada the notice is to be given to the Minister of Railways.' In both countries, under and by virtue of their legislation, inspectors are to be employed and inspection is provided for, with this marked difference, that in Canada our inspectors perform all their duties when they inspect the cars and the devices made to protect the lives of the railway employees. But in the United States their legislation provides that the members of the Interstate Commerce Commission shall enforce the law. In each country penalties are provided for the infringement of the laws, or for disobedience of orders of, in the one country the Interstate Commerce Commission, in the other of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Section 30 of the Canadian Act, subsection 3, says that :
The Board of Railway Commissioners may by regulation provide penalties where none are provided by the Railway Act, but these penalties shall not exceed one hundred dollars.
Now, Sir, I have pointed out where, in the main, the laws of the two countries are similar. I have said that in the United States their laws better provide for the enforcement of their statutes and regulations. As I have said, our board has no power to lay any information, to bring any action against an offender. The Act I have referred to as the ' United States Safety Appliance Acts ' provides as follows:
That any such common carrier using any locomotive engine, running any train, or hauling or permitting to be hauled or used on its line any car in violation of any of the provisions of this Act, shall be liable to a penalty of $100 for each and every such violation, to be recovered in suit or suits to be brought by the United States district attorney in the Mr. MILLER.
district court of the United States having jurisdiction in the locality where such violation shall have been committed; and it shall be the duty of such district attorney to bring such suits upon duly verified information being lodged with him of such violation having occurred; and it shall also be the duty of the Interstate Commerce Commission to lodge with the proper district attorneys information of any such violations as may come to its knowledge.
These two sections disclose a most important difference between the legislation of our own country and that of the United States. In Canada it is not the duty of any member of our Board of Railway Commissioners, nor is it the duty of any employee, or member of the staff of the board, to bring any action, or to lay any information. It rests with the person aggrieved, or with some other person nut having any personal interest in the matter. It is reasonable to suppose that a railway employee will hesitate very much about bringing action against a railway company because of the fact that one of the likely consequences will be the loss of his situation, thus depriving him of his employment. The United States Sundry Civil Act, passed June 28, 1902, authorizes the Interstate Commerce Commission to employ inspectors to execute and enforce the requirements of the Safety Appliance Acts. The Interstate Commerce Commission is authorized, then, to employ and does employ two sets of inspectors, one to make a careful inspection of the cars used by the various railway companies of the republic, and the other to see to the enforcement of the laws that they provide. There is, Sir, other important legislation in the United States that we do not have in Canada. It is not upon our statute-books, it is not contained in any order of the Railway Commission, and I do not think that our Board of Railway Commissioners have any power to make such an order or law to limit the hours of service. The United States have an Act, passed on the 4th March, 1907, one section of which reads as follows:
That it shall be unlawful for any common carrier, its officers or agents, subject to this Act to require or permit any employee subject to this Act to be or remain on duty for a longer period than sixteen consecutive hours, and whenever such employee of such common carrier shall have been continuously on duty for sixteen hours he shall be relieved and not required or permitted to again go on duty until he has had at least ten consecutive hours off duty; and no such employee who has been on duty sixteen hours in the aggregate in any twenty-four hour period shall be required or permitted to continue or again go on duty without having had at least eight consecutive hours off duty; provided, that no operator, train despatcher, or other employee who by use of the telegraph or telephone despatches, reports, transmits, re-

oeives or delivers orders appertaining to or affecting train movements shall be required or permitted to be or remain on duty for a longer period than nine hours in a twenty-four hour period in towers, offices, places and stations continuously operated night .and day, nor for a longer period than thirteen hours in towers, offices, places and stations operated only during the daytime, except in ease of emergency, when the employees named in this proviso may- be permitted to be and remain on duty for four additional hours in a twenty-four hour period not exceeding three days in any week.
The next section provides as follows:
And it shall also be the duty of the Interstate Commerce Commission to lodge with the proper district attorneys information of any such violation as may come to its knowledge. In all prosecutions under this Act the common carrier shall be deemed to have had knowledge of all acts of all its officers and agents.
I think that is very important legislation. I am informed that in Canada the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway have regulations of their own for limiting, in some such way. $,s the United States statute does, the hours of labour. I do not Know how carefully or how carelessly the orders of these two railway companies are enforced, and I do not know whether any other Canadian railways except these two have such regulations. 1 believe that a few years ago the Canadian Board of Railway Commissioners was asked to make an order, or to obtain legislation, limiting the hours of labour in some such way as the American statute does. I am told that the engineers and firemen were in favour of such legislation, but that the conductors and trainmen, meaning, I suppose, the brakesmen, were opposed to any such legislation. It might very well be that the employees of a railway company are opposed to any statute which will limit their hours of labour. It is very natural that a conductor, or brakeman, for the sake of making the greatest possible earnings, of receiving the utmost wages, would be willing to work longer hours than he ought to be permitted to work, having consideration for his own safety, those who labour with him and those riding upon the trains of which he is in charge. I think that oftentimes, when an accident occurs upon a Canadian railway, if it has teen due to the negligence of any railway employees, the excuse or reason is given that the employee had been on duty so many hours that he could not possibly be in his normal condition, or as alert as he otherwise would have been. There is loo rather novel legislation upon the American statute-books, passed in February, 1905, and I will quote shortly from that Act. This Act, passed in 1905 by the American Congress, since amended and still remaining upon the 124i
statute-books, is entitled ' An Act to promote Security of Travel upon Railroads engaged in the Interstate Commerce and to encourage the saving of Life.' The first part of the first section of the Act reads as follows:
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, that the President of the United States be and is hereby authorized to cause to be prepared bronze medals of honour, with suitable emblematio devices, which shall be bestowed upon any persons who shall hereafter, by extreme daring, endanger their own lives in saving, or endeavouring to save, lives from any wreck, d'saster, or grave accident, or in preventing or endeavouring to prevent such wreck, disaster, or grave accident, upon any railroad within the United States engaged in interstate commerce.
If we had not read the title of that Act. one might suppose it to be merely philanthropy. The title indicates the purpose of the United States Congress had in view in passing the Act:	An Act to promote the security of travel upon railroads engaged in interstate commerce and to encourage the saving of life. It may be questioned as to whether or not that would effect the desired end and yet if the United States Congress think it wise to pass it and allow it to remain on the statute-book after six years experience, it is perhaps worthy of our consideration. Complaint has also been made that many of our Canadian railways do not employ a sufficient number of section men to keep the track in condition so as to ensure the greatest degree of safety to employees and the travelling public, and that matter might perhaps be worthy of inquiry. I am pleased to note that in Canada and in the United States as well, those whose duty it is to protect railway employees are encouraged, with the result of their efforts. At page 352 of the renort of our own railway commissioners, Mr. A. J. Nixon, chief traffic officer, reports that last year 51 passengers, 194 employees and 211 other persons were killed; while 211 passengers, 745 employees and 167 other persons were injured. Mr. Nixon says:
Investigations were made by the board's inspectors m 282 of the above cases and reports on same were handed to the board. General' inspections have been made by the inspectors of equipment, stations and crossings of all railways under the jurisdiction of the board..
The commissioners at page 112 say:
The schedules to the report of the chief operating officer give a full analysis of the accidents during the year, which would have been a record one had it not been for the unfortunate accident at Spanish river. This has been and is being most carefully investigated.

I turn to the last obtainable report of the United States Interstate Commerce Commission and I read:
As showing the care with which the safety appliances demanded by the law- are being maintained, it may be noted that while the railroads dispensed with the services of a great many emjdoyees to meet the economies necessitated by falling oil of business in 1907, the force of men employed to maintain safety appliances suffered the least curtailment of any. As a result the condition of equipment continued to improve during the slack period of 1908-9, the year just closed, showing the least percentage of defective equipment of any year since the law became operative, notwithstanding that the number of cars examined by our inspectors was 125,000 greater than in any previous year. As indicating the great improvement that has taken place within the past five years, it may be stated that the defects per 1,000 cars inspected in 1905 numbered 309-56, while for the year 1909 the figure is 71-65.
The report of the Interstate Commerce Commission indicate that their efforts are meeting with great success and that their inspection of cars and equipment is very thorough. I trust that the inspection by the inspectors of our own board is equally thorough. Let me call the attention of the House, but particularly the Minister of Railways to three or four things: In the first place I think our Railway Act might well be amended after consultation between the Minister of Railways and the Board of Railway Commissioners, so as to give us something like the same machinery for enforcing our laws and regulations as prevails under the legislation of the United States. Notwithstanding that so_me of the employees oppose this, while others favour it, I believe it would be a step in advance if our Railway Act did contain provision that would limit as the United States law does, the hours of service of trainmen and of telegraph and telephone despatchers. Then, there is legislation in the United States as to the granting of medals, and the Minister of Railways might deem that worthy of consideration. I have no desire to push the resolution unduly, my object being to bring the matter to the attention of parliament, of the Minister of Railways, and of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways).
speechtext:
The subject brought to the attention of the House by my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) is very important. In this country railway operation is much more difficult than in a country where there are not the same extremes of heat and cold. The accidents to employees mav be divided into several classes, among which might be mentioned cases in which the employee becomes so accustomed to his work that he ignores conditions of danger, and no care on the part of the company can prevent Mr. MILLER.
accidents from that cause. I have in my mind a case where a few weeks ago two employees were working on a car in the yard, and they carelessly stepped in front of an incoming express and both were killed. No sort of regulation or rule can protect men against their own carelessness. Then, a number of employees are killed while on board trains as crews. Accidents arise from defects in the track or roadway, and others are caused by the neglect of some officials connected with the operation of trains. Then there are accidents arising from defective rolling stock. The extremes of heat and cold in Canada render railway operation very difficult. To-day the track may be in good condition and examine it carefully as you will you find no defect, but a heavy frost comes followed by a thaw, and the track heaves and accidents occur. It is almost impossible in a climate like ours to prevent this, but I think I may say that in recent years more care has been taken than formerly. As to the number of section men that should be employed, I have studied that matter somewhat carefully and while there is a difference in the number of section men employed on different railways, the differing traffic of the lines may account for that. On a trunk line carrying heavy traffic a greater number of men per track mile are needed than on a branch line on which there is only one or two trains a day. It is difficult to make a law that would apply absolutely to the number of men that should be employed per section on a railway. The sections differ in length, some are longer than others, and one section will carry more traffic than another section.
I discussed that at some length with one of the officials of the brotherhoods recently, and he agreed with me in thinking that in Canada at the present time a sufficient number of men on the average was being employed to keep the tracks in fairly good condition, considering the traffic on the various lines. But this must be remembered, that the brotherhoods themselves _ have a very strong influence in determining how many men shall be employed, their hours of labour, and all that kind of thing. No railway company is allowed itself to say how many hours a man shall work, and scarcely how many men shall work. The railway companies have to make contracts with the various brotherhoods as to all these things, and my experience is that they arrive at a pretty fair solution as far as the men and the keeping of the tracks in condition are concerned. Then, in the last few years the rolling stock has become so much heavier and the trains so much longer that a heavier rail and a better roadbed are required than was the case a few years ago. The rolling stock also is being improved very rapidly. It is heavier than it was, and no new rolling stock is allowed

to come out of the shop, and to be used unless it complies with the requirements of the Railway Commission, and all old rolling stock is being brought up to those requirements. Then, there has been a great advance in the last few years in the protection of railway men by the introduction of the automatic brake and other improved appliances; so that if the railway employee is careful, unless- there is a collision or a broken rail, his life is not nearly such a risky one as it was a few years ago. The requirements of the Commissioners are stringent and even if they were not the rolling stock of Canadian railways has to be up to the standard in these respects, because it is- interchangeable with the rolling stock of United States railways, and a Canadian car that does not comply with the conditions of the laws prevailing in the United States is not allowed to go on a United States road. Our railways' are in such close intercourse with the United States railways that even if we had no regulations of our Board of Railway Commissioners, we would be compelled to comply with certain regulations imposed by the Interstate Commerce Commission. Then, every railway company is practically compelled to make arrangements with the different brotherhoods as to the terms under which they shall work. It is a mistake now to suppose that -all these arrangements have reference to wages. The schedules agreed upon cover every phase of a man's employment-his hours of labour, his holidays, his transportation, what he shall do, when he shall do it, how muen he shall get if he does something else. Of this I know something, because I have had to make some of these arrangements. What we are after in Canada are results. I am not so sure about medals which might encourage philanthropic effort to rescue those who are injured. I would rather do something to obviate the use of medals by reducing the number of accidents. What can we do? The United States have various laws. Their conditions are different from ours. Their best railways have double tracks. The Grand Trunk railway has double tracks on its main line. On these double track lines the accidents are reduced to a minimum; and I think that a careful examination of the records, bearing in mind that the greater amount of business in Canada is done on single track lines, will show that there are far fewer accidents in Canada than in the United States. I think that on the whole greater care is exercised in Canada than across the line, and that rather than the making of laws tends to the reduction of accidents. I think that in Canada we perhaps make the mistake of thinking that the cure for any evil that exists is to pass a law of some kind and then forget it. What we are trying to do is to work out,
through a practical board which has much greater power than the United States board, something that will encourage care on the part of the railway employees as well as on the part of the railway companies. Has this result been attained? To a large extent it has. After all, it is not so much a question of the laws that we should put on the statute-book as a question of the quality of the men engaged in the work. I nave had a good deal to do with the railway men in Canada, and I believe I am safe in saying that in any country there is no more intelligent class of men employed than we find on the railways; and the more we encourage such men to go into the work on our great railway systems, the fewer will be the accidents and the greater will be the satisfaction of the people. The Railway Commission In Canada is in a somewhat different position from the Interstate Commission in the United States. Under their system the railways are chartered by the states, and the Interstate Commission has power only to regulate traffic that passes from one state to another, not traffic in each state. It has a greater power than our commission as to prosecution, and it is more in line with their constitution for the federal power to undertake prosecutions than it is with us in Canada, where the enforcement of the laws is left largely to provincial jurisdiction. In the United States there is a fine for a violation of the law. We have not the same procedure or the same fine, but if a railway company is found running a car against the order of -the board, it is not allowed to run that car again until it conforms to the regulations of the board. No company dares to break that order, because the board can go much further; it can prevent the railway company doing any business until it complies with the order of the board. It could issue an order that this railway could not run a train except with properly equipped cars and that becomes an order of the court. I think that would be equivalent to an injunction issued against any one to prevent his doing something. So that the power given our railway board is much greater that that possessed by the United States board. There are appeals from the decisions of the latter in every case to some court or another.
Last year our Board of Railway Commissioners disposed of over 3,000 oases without almost a hearing, without any formality, in many cases after hearing the story by mail; and the results in Canada, whatever our laws may be, are as beneficial, or more so, than the results in the United States with their laws. But if we can improve our laws in any way, I should be delighted to do so. The Board of Railway Commissioners has appointed a certain number of inspectors in every section of the

Dominion, and whenever an accident occurs, one of these inspectors is on the ground as rapidly as he can get there.
Have the inspectors the authority to prosecute, and if not, would it not be well that they should have it ?

That is a question for argument. The result is what we are after, and I believe that we have better results than in the United States. Although our inspectors have not the power to prosecute, they can be ordered to lay an information, but that is not part of their duty Under our system, when an accident occurs, if the circumstances warrant such an investigation, the coroner holds an inquest, and where there is any negligence, the coroner's jury lays the foundation for criminal prosecution and the provincial authorities prosecute the party supposed to be guilty. Therefore, I am not sme that we would gain anything in that regard, although the suggestion might be worth thinking about. His suggestion would make it imperative to institute a prosecution before some authority, but possibly that would take out of the hands of the coroner and the provincial authorities the machinery amply provided in cases of fatal accidents. We have appointed these in specters, they are on the ground at every point, and give a full report of every accident. They do not make a speciality of saying that the company is guilty, but they go along these lines, if I remember rightly. Was the accident caused by a spread rail, -a broken wheel, a misinterpreted order, by wrong orders, by something wrong with the locomotive, by some fault in the rolling stock or negligence of somebody. And they investigate on the spot, where every one knows all about the circumstances, and ascertain just what the reason was, and that practically tells us, so far as it can be told, who is the party in fault. This information is compiled and brought to the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the hoard immediately takes the matter up with the company, if the accident was due to a faulty track, the board discusses that fairly with the company, and the result has been that tranks are kept in better condition. The railway company, knowing the workings of our railway board, in their own interests as well as the interests of tire public, are very careful that all rolling stock now undergoes a thorough inspection. They do not even trust their own officials to inspect the cars, but there are certain companies which make a business of inspecting rolling stock, and the railway company engage their services. When an order is given for rolliny stock, such as cars or locomotives, these are not taken over by the railway company until these experts, independent 'Mr. GRAHAM
of either the manufacturer or the purchaser, give a certificate that the stock is up to standard and specification, and fit tor service.
There is a question discussed a good deal in the House and the country, and that is as .to the further inspection of locomotives in this way, and I think my hon, friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), has a Bill introduced in this connection. Railway men say that a locomotive may appear to be in good condition in the shop, but after it is on the road a little time, something becomes faulty to a greater or lesser degree. They think it would be in the interest of all parties, if there were inspectors who had authority at any time to jump on board one of these locomotives and inspect it. They think also that if there were men possibly who would jump on >a train more frequently than at present and inspect the rolling stock in motion, that would be a good thing. If the board has not the power now to do that-and I am not sure that it has not-we may give it to them. My opinion, however, is that the board has the power under the Act to engage any official it sees fit to employ for any purpose whatever. However, the department will be glad to receive any suggestions to perfect the Act, because whatever will protect the employee, will of course, protect the traveller as well. We have a young country with a large expanse of territory and a great mileage of railways developing very rapidly and with our climatic condition's and lather difficulties to face we have a greater problem to solv than they have to the south and much greater than they have in Europe. Still we are making good progress', and we are glad to take suggestions a.s to how we can improve conditions.
We hear a great deal about the Act being defective in protecting live stock from being killed by trains. As a matter of fact the original idea of all these provisions about fencing, &c., was not so much to protect the cattle as to protect the employees and passengers. The chief thing in the minds of the framers of the Act was, tha if cattle or horses or other obstructions got on the track, there was liable to be death for the employees and passengers and destruction of property. But we are asked now to legislate rather with the view of protecting the animals who get on the tracks from being killed. Of course, the one works as well as the other, but there is a double reason why cattle should be kept off the tracks, first, for the protection of the passengers and employees, and secondly for the protection of the animals themselves. That is one of the reasons why the old style of having a pit at the crossings, which is the only absolute way of keeping animals off the tracks, has been abandoned.

The employees 'Complained that there was danger to the animals getting into these pits and thus throwing the locomotive off the tracks and injuring the employees and perhaps the passengers as well.
Are there any statistics to show the percentage of accidents in that way ?

At the time these pits were in vogue, our statistics were veTy, incomplete, but the consensus of opinio is that these pits are not the safest kind of cattle guards to have on the railway. We are doing a great deal for the protection of life. Our rolling stock is being rapidly brought up to as high a standard as possible. It is being tested as it never was before.	Our roadways in
Canada are in better condition to-day thau ever. More money is being spent, heavier rails are being used, double track is being installed, inter switching devices which wer not known a few years ago are being installed.
Level crossings are being protected by hundreds as never before. In all of these things we are moving along pretty well in the way of protecting life in all possible positions. But we live pretty fast in this country and are moving rapidly. Those of us who are most eloquent about the danger of trains are the most anxious to get on the fastest trains we can, and those who insist that we must not allow trains to travel rapidly through villages or towns are loudly indignant if a train even slows up in passing through a village. Our rolling stock and roadbeds are being improved, and, as far as we are concerned we are anxious that lives of passengers and trainmen and public should be protected to the fullest extent, and in that respect we are glad to receive suggestions from the hon. member or any one else.

After the remarks of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), it may he unnecessary to add anything to what has been said, but this question of industrial accidents is one of such very great importance to the nation not less than to labour that I feel I should like to add just a word or two to what has been said by the mover of the resolution and the Minister of Railways.
In the first place, I should like to endorse what the minister said when he pointed out that although as the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) has said, the United States has excellent legislation. has put many statutes on the books, the result goes to show that there are fewer persons killed on the railways of the Dominion of Canada than on the railways of the United States in proportion to the total
number of employees in the respective countries. I have here statistics which have been carefully compiled from the railway statistics of the Dominion, from the reports of the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States, and from the Home Office reports of Great Britain, and these statistics throw a good deal of light upon the effect of legislation and the enforcement of legislation in the different countries. I regret to notice that the showing as to the number of accidents is even larger than that indicated by the mover of the resolution. In his resolution he has stated that it appears that one in every 199 trainmen was killed in Canada, and one in every 33 injured. That seems a very laTge percentage, but the records, unfortunately, show that the percentage is even larger than that, that the number of employees killed on railways in any one year is more than one in every 199, and the number injured than one in every 33. That, of course refers to all the railways of the Dominion.
