It will be seen that the percentage of employees killed in Canada in proportion to the total number employed is lower than in the United States. The difference, on the other hand, between Great Britain and Canada and the United States, is very marked. This difference is, of course, doubtless accounted for in part by the facts mentioned bv the Minister of Railways, that we have in this country climatic con-

3a3o
ditions to contend with, vast stretches of territory which are much more difficult to safeguard and protect, and considering the difficulties and problems that nature presents in this country, it is natural to expect that the percentage will be considerably higher than in the old land.
These figures will come somewhat as a surprise to the public generally, who can hardly be familiar with the extent to which industrial accidents occur with respect to railway employees of the different countries.
Summarizing the figures, it would appear that the total number of Tailway employees killed in Canada in the past three years has been 633, the total number injured 3,134, making a total of 3,767 fatal and non-fatal accidents in this period.
Giving the House the figures in another form, of the 19,443 trainmen in Canada in 1909, 1 out of every 172 was killed, and one out of every 28 injured. In 1908 the proportion of killed was one out of every 168, and of injured one out of every 23. In 1907 the proportion of killed was one out of every 136 and of injured one out of every 26. ' '
My bon. friend from East Grey has referred particularly to' the United States legislation, and to results which have been achieved there. The figures I have read to the House go to show that with such legislation as we have, and with the facilities afforded particularly in connection with the Railway Commission, the number of accidents are fewer, and the number of fatalities are fewer, relatively. But the following figures taken from reliable sources in the United States, will help to bring out the significance of the loss of life in that country. I think they are worthy of being read to this House, because they help to show what is inevitably incident to the calling of railway employees. Mr. Daniel L. Cease, in an address before the fourth annual meeting of the American Association for labour legislation, in St. Louis, December 29, 1910, says:
The railroad casualty statistics for the last year showed that 9 men were killed each 24 hours, and that 1 was injured or killed every 7 minutes. One man was killed for each 205 employed, and one was injured for every 9 employed. The working life of a brakemam is estimated at only 7 years.
Frill statistics covering other occupations are lacking, but the miners claim that 4 men are _ killed in America to one in Europe; and it is admitted that mining ordinarily and normally ought to be accomplished with less danger here than abroad.
Then I find the following statement, which is no less striking, in a book entitled ' Perils of Peace,' published in 1906, by the Mr. KING.
American Institute of Social Service. I will read one or two paragraphs:
Our peaceful avocations cost more lives every two days than all that we lost in battle during our war in Spain. It has been pointed out that the Pennsylvania coal fields alone furnish ' an industrial Bull Run ' annually.
In these piping times of peace, we in the United States kill in four years some 80,000 people more than all who fell in battle and died of wounds, on both sides, during the four years of our civil war; that is, in the same length of time, we are now killing 53 per cent more people than two great armies could destroy, equipped with all the weapons that ingenuity could then devise, and making destruction their eager business.
We are killing more than twice as many every year as perished by violence in both the French and English armies during the three years of the Crimean war. There are more killed and wounded on our railroads every year than the entire losses of the Boer war on both sides in three years.
That is a record of loss of life which ought to impress the minds of all who take an interest in the preservation of a people. Speaking only of the railroads in the United States, we are told that there are more killed and wounded every year than the entire losses of the Boer war on both sides in three years. Then I have here a reference taken from an article on the loss of life on the United States railways, by John W. Gitterman, which appeared recently in McClure's magazine for June, 1910:
It is difficult to realize that in the fiscal year 1908 the railroads of the United States killed, in addition to passengers, 3,470 of their own employees, an average of 328 deaths each month since 1903.
Injuries are twenty times more numerous than deaths. Last year six and four-tenths per cent of all the railway employees in the United States were injured: thus the chances are that no man can escape accident for nine years. No wonder that most of the life insurance companies refuse to insure a railroad man on any terms, while in any sort of company a switchman can be insured only at a rating twenty years in advance of his actual age.
Where, twenty years ago, the employee had an even chance of remaining uninjured for more than fifteen years, his expectation has sunk nearly to eight. In spite of double-tracking and safety devices and palliative legislation, matters have come to such a pass that if the injured of one bad year could all wait in line before one hospital door, the queue, if laid side by side, would make a row nearly two miles long.
In twenty-one years the percentage of employees killed or injured on the railroads of the United States has nearly doubled. At the present rate it would take only seventeen years to kill or injure all the employees now on the rolls. If the number of railroad employees remains constant for fifteen years, 1,300,000 men, at the present mortality rate, will be

killed or injured. But the number, of course, will greatly increase. It is, therefore, probably no exaggeration to say that, unless the railroads radically improve their present methods of safeguarding their employees' lives, they will either kill or injure, within the next fifteen years, not far from 2,000,000 men.
These figures are reliable statistics, illustrating conditions on United States railways, notwithstanding the excellent legislation to which my hon. friend has made reference. I might make mention of one feature which he seemed to regard as important and as existing in the United States, but wanting in this country. My hon. friend referred to an Act to promote the security of travellers and tend to the safety of life, and if I understood him rightly, medals of honour were to be awarded under that statute by the President of the United States. Two or three years ago his late Majesty King Edward offered a similar medal for precisely the same purpose, and extended this offer to the selfgoverning dominions of the British Empire. So at the presnt time any man in Canada who performs an heroic act of that kind, is entitled to receive, not a medal from some local authority, but to receive the Albert medal,_ as it is called, from His Majesty the King. In fact, one such medal was awarded last year to a Canadian. I have here an account given in the Labour ' Gazette,' of 1910, page 1350, of the award of a medal to Mr. Thomas Reynolds, in connection with the Spanish river accident. This communication is dated Whitehall, April 25, 1910, and has the following:
The King has been pleased to confer the Albert medal of the first class upon Mr. Thomas Reynolds, railway conductor, of North Bay, Ontario, Canada, for conspicuous gallantry in saving the lives of eleven persons on the occasion of the disaster on the Canadian Pacific railway at the Spanish river bridge, near Webbwood, Ont., on January 21 last, as detailed below.
Then follows an account of the action performed by Conductor Reynolds, and concludes :
The presentation of the medal, in the name of His Majesty, was performed by His Excellency the Governor General of Canada at Montreal, on the 16th ultimo.
I believe it has since been arranged that this medal shall be presented for acts of heroism on the part of miners and men in other industries, as well as on railways, so that in so far as marks of honour or royal recognition may prove an incentive to acts of heroism a very strong incentive _ has been provided by HTs late Majesty. But while I think the hon. member for Grey has rendered a great service to the workingmen of
this country in bringing out the facts which he has brought out in connection with industrial accidents, he might have rendered even a greater service if he had extended the scope of his resolution beyond industrial accidents on railways, to cover loss of life and limb which occurs in industrial accidents generally. This is a matter to which the Department of Labour has been devoting some attention for years past. By gathering from as many sources as possible the record of industrial accidents occurring in the Dominion we are in a position to lay , before the country a statement of what the loss of life in industry amounts to in Canada. By referring to the annual report of the Department of Labour hon. members will find there statistical tables showing the number of fatal and non-fatal accidents which have occurred in Canada during the last few years. We have the figures for 1904, 1905, 1908, 1907, 1908, 1909 and 1910. These figures are gathered from a great variety of sources, from the press of the country, from labour organizations, from railway boards and from any sources which the department can find it possible to communicate with. Whenever the account of a fatal accident to a workingman in the course of his employment is brought to the attention of the department, the department communicates with responsible parties and obtains accurate information with regard to the accident. It is from information gathered in this way that these statistics relating to deaths have been compiled. Without attempting to -give the House in any detail the figures contained in these tables, 1 might just mention that, taking industrial callings generally, the figures go to show that in the year 1907, having regard to the different trades and callings, 1,353 persons were killed outright in the course of their employment; in 1908, 1,272, and in 1909, 1,278; or an average of about 1,300 a year of deaths of workingmen in Canada occasioned in the course of their employment. I emphasize these last words because it is only such accidents as occur to men while they are actually working that are recorded in these statistics. These are necessarily incomplete. In a very large number of cases employers naturally try to conceal from the public the fact that men have been killed in their particular businesses and there are men killed in trades of whom the public never learns. Then again there are men who meet with accidents and are taken to hospitals or their homes where they die later. The department may get an account of the accident but never learns of the death of the man. I think we would be safe in saying that if we get a record of half the accidents we are doing about as much as can be expected. But,

assuming that we get more than half, assuming that we get about three-fifths, the showing would be that something like
2.000	workingmen are killed outright in Canada every year in the course of their employment. That does not include, for example, men who. may be going to work and being killed by * a train but includes only men killed while actually working at their particular trades. The number whose industrial efficiency is impaired for all time through loss of limb or through some other impairment of physical health is at least five times the number killed. Hence it would appear that two thousand of the workers of the Dominion are killed outright every year, and that there are 10,000 whose industrial efficiency is impaired for all time. Take that average for a period of ten years and what is the result? As far as Canada is concerned we kill outright in our industries 20,000 men and we permanently impair the industrial efficiency of something like 100,000 others. That is a tremendous loss to the nation. In ten years
20.000	of its wealth producers killed and
100.000	whose industrial efficiency is impaired for all time to come.
What distinction do you make between killed and killed outright?

I did not intend to draw any particular distinction. I presume that what I had in my mind when I said killed outright was that a man was killed immediately upon the accident occurring. A man who is injured and dies in a couple of weeks would not be killed outright.
I understand it is from secondary causes.

However, the point I was trying to make is that while we are trying to conserve our natural resources, which is a worthy object, the conservation of human life, of human resources, is something of equal if not greater importance not only from the point of view of economic wealth but also from that of national strength and well being; and to the extent which the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) has helped to direct public attention to the significance of loss of life in that connection and the necessity for the state doing all in its power to help to reduce this death toll and this massacre of human beings he has rendered to the people and especially to the working classes of this country a very, very great service.
But there is one other phase of the question which I would like to bring to the attention of the House. It is not mentioned in the resolution of my hon. friend but it is suggested by the figures which I have given. My hon. friend said spme-thing about the appointing of a prosecutor Mr. KING.
on the part of the state to prosecute railway companies and, in that connection, he has drawn attention to the fact that the compensation which is to come in the case of loss of life or loss of limb frequently comes only as the result of some legal action. I think it is worth the while of members of this House and of other legislators in the country to consider whether or not there is not a necessity for remedying in some shape or form that circumstance. We can say with certainty at this', moment that a year hence another 2,00b lives will be swept off the list of workers in Canada, and in another year there will be 10,000 men whose industrial efficiency will be permanently impaired as a consequence of accidents occurring in the callings in which they are engaged. We know that loss of life is incident to a calling itself. If that is so does it not appear that in some way the industry itself should be made to bear what is inevitable to it? Take the case of a railway company with its cars; so much is allowed for broken cars or for repairing damage done to cars. I am just suggesting this thought because it is a large subject and it would involve much consideration before anything in the shape of legislation could be based upon it, but it is not worth considering whether human life is not entitled to the same amount of protection and kind of provision as is afforded to what is part of the rolling stock of a company and whether in some way the industry could not be made to bear part of the cost of its inevitable loss of life and limb with the result that those who are left behind, those who belong to the family of the man who may have been killed outright, shall not, in consequence of his death, be put in the position that in order to get some compensation for the loss of his life they must enter upon litigation and add to the distress which they already have? These are the suggestions that I thought I should like to make because I think they are points which are attracting considerable attention among the industrial workers of the country and, having regard for the conservation of human life, for the upbuilding of the strength of the nation as a whole, too much attention cannot be given to a very serious aspect of this very serious question.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose at this hour to add very many words to what has already been said. It appears to me that the importance of this subject entirely warrants my hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) in bringing it to the attention oi the House. The remarks made by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Railways and Canals show that they both had notice that this motion would be pre-

sented this evening while some of ns who desired to speak on it had no such notice.
The only notice I had was seeing the resolution on the Order Paper and my hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) had precisely the same opportunity.

I must congratulate the Minister of Labour upon his great ability in delivering such a well prepared speech without any previous study. The Minister of Labour took considerable pains to gather details of the appalling loss of life, but I regret that he is not in a position to suggest a remedy, as his duty would seem to demand. He told us he had been collecting statistics for years, but to what purpose is all this discussion if we let it drop without taking any action. The Minister of Railways has no suggestion to make, the Minister of Labour has no suggestion to make, but the subject seems to be of sufficient importance to warrant the government entering into a special investigation as to the means that should be adopted to lessen the deplorable loss of life which we have heard so much about. No reason is given why the fatalities are higher in Canada than in England, and it seems possible that our death rate from this cause could be lessened if proper methods were adopted. The Minister of Railways told us that we were improving all the time, but I know from mingling with railway men day after day that a great many of them complain that they are compelled to serve too long hours, that they have not sufficient time for rest between runs, and some railways have so many branches that a man is sent out and is sometimes on the go for three or four days with practically no rest except what he may obtain when his train is on a siding. The railway men of this country will expect the government to take some reasonable action on which to base legislation with a view of lessening the appalling death toll on Canadian railways.

There was no intent of discourtesy on my part in not informing hon. members that the resolution would be gone on with to-night because I did not know myself that it would be called. I gave no notice to the Minister of Labour. He asked me to-day if I would go on and I told him I would if the motion were reached. Neither did I give notice to the Minister of Railways. One of the whips on the other side asked me if I would proceed with the resolution to-night and I told him I would if it were reached.
I think it was to-night that I asked vou if you would go on with the motion?

It was. I somewhat agree with the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers) that we should have more than words and that there is something that should be done in this direction. I am glad to hear from the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Labour that in Canada as great interest is being taken in this question as in the United States, and that we are doing much, as they are, in prevent-itive measures. Still, I think there is something more that could be done. The Minister of Railways told us that Canada was a very difficult country in which to operate railway trains, because of the climatic conditions, and my answer to that is that the greater the difficulty the greater the effort should be to overcome that difficulty. He told us that certain accidents were due to the neglect of somebody connected with train operation, but in the United States, there is not only legislation to punish that somebody but there are officials whose duty it is to enforce it. That we have not in Canada. The minister also told us that accidents occurred through faulty rolling stock, but he himself gave the evidence that greater care is taken in the United States than in Canada because he told us that certain cars which were used in Canada would not be permitted in the United States and particularly in the state of New York. It is not sufficient protection for Canadian employees that faulty cars of Canadian railroads will not be interchanged by American railroads, because if the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk Pacific had such defective cars they need not send them to the United States ; there is nothing in the world to prevent them sending them through Canada to the Pacific coast. The Minister of Railways told us that the coroner was the first to take action, and that the Board of Railway Commissioners followed, but the proper time to prevent accidents is before there is an accident, and before the coroner is called in. The Minister of Railways also told us that it doesn't do any good to pass a law and then forget it, and that is exactly [DOT]my contention. In the United States they pass the law, and then they appoint an official whose duty it is to see that nobody is allowed to forget or neglect that law.
As to the hours of labour, the Minister of Railways has pointed out that there is always an arrangement between the railway brotherhoods and the railway companies that limits the hours of labour. One of the officials of the Board of Railway Commissioners in Ottawa informed me that some years ago there was a request from the railway men for legislation to limit the hours of labour, and that it was supported by the engineers and firemen and opposed by the trainmen. The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers) has stated that the railway men in his city have complained of the long hours that they have to work, and of the disastrous consequences to them

and to the people in the trains. It is not sufficient protection to the employees and the passengers that an arrangement has taken place between the brotherhoods and the railway companies. That is too elastic; it is too easy to evade it, and many a railway employee is tempted, by the larger wage he receives, to work longer hours than his own safety or the safety of those in his charge ought to allow him to do. I contend that, though it is a fortunate thing, and a thing on which, perhaps, we may congratulate ourselves, that the percentage of accidents is somewhat greater in the United States than in Canada, yet we may safely copy their legislation in so far as safety appliances and limiting the hours of labour, and particularly means of enforcing legislation are concerned. These are two matters of importance, which, if attended to, would reduce the number of accidents. Mr. Speaker, having brought this matter to the attention of the House, I would, with your permission, withdraw the resolution.

Why should the hon. gentleman do that, if he wants an expression of the opinion of the House? It is probable that the House would pass the resolution, and then we would be put in possession of the information sought for.
I am willing that that should be done.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman whether there is any information as to the percentage of accidents per mile of railway operated in Canada by the different railway companies?
If there is any such information, I am not aware of it.
Perhaps the Minister of Labour has that information?
I cannot say that the statistics are compiled in that way. I think it would be easy to so compile them, from the records we have from the railways.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the motion is not withdrawn, I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
Mr. MARTIN (St. Mary's, Montreal) moved second reading of Bill (No. 4) to amend the Railway Act.
This is a very important Bill, and it should hardly be passed at this hour. It was brought up last session or the session before, and a great deal of objection was taken to it in the House.
I have an amendment to move in committee to meet the objection.
I think it should stand until we get some notice of the amendment.

Last year the Bill was referred to the Committee on Railways and Canals. It was said that the workingmen had never asked for it, but this year a large delegation of the men working on the Canadian Pacific railway have asked for it. It is proposed by the amendment that the men should be paid every two weeks. We know that if men have to work for a month without getting their pay they have to buy many things on credit. So I think the Bill is quite reasonable.
I would suggest that the Bill be read a second time and be sent to the Railway Committee, where both the railway men and the railway companies could be heard.

This is a public Bill, and I do not see why we should refer it to the Railway Committee. It was referred to that committee last year, and the railway companies represented that the workingmen had never asked for this. Well, I have a letter here, and a petition signed by over 1,000 men, and this petition was signed five years ago. The answer which Sir Thomas Shaughnessy . gave was that as soon as the Angus shops would be built, and the Montreal Bank have a branch at the works, the company would be willing to pay every two weeks. That was the answer given by the Canadian Pacific railway four years ago, but last year in the-Railway Committee they said that the workingmen had never asked for it. I do not see, therefore, why we should refer this Bill to that committee. We all know what happens when a Bill is referred to it.
The hon. gentleman has no right to say that in the face of the fact he has just given.

I have the letter and petition here. I do not want to mention the name of the writer of that letter, because he has worked for the company 25 years, and if I disclosed his name he would be discharged. Here is the petition which was circulated around these shops. I have counted the number of names, and I find that 1,071 men have signed it. There is no reason why these men should not be paid every two weeks; and if this Bill be referred to the Railway Committee, it will not pass this session. This is the fourth session I have brought it up. All I ask is that any railway company, which has been given any aid by the government, should pay its employees every two weeks.
An. hon. MEMBER. How many men have signed?
Some 1,200 or 1,300, or 89 per cent of those employed.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time.
Mr. MARTIN (St. Mary's) moved that the House go into committee on the Bill.

This matter should be referred to the Railway Committee. Last year it was given a very full discussion in that committee; and if we are going to change the decision then arrived at, both parties ought to be given a hearing before the committee. It was said then that the men were not making any demand for this change; and we must bear in mind that a railway company is very different from another corporation. Any company in which I am interested pays its men every two [DOT]weeks, and it is easy for us to do so because the men are within reach. But with a large railway company the case is different. The Grand Trunk railway for instance extends all over this country, and has to make up its pay sheets in Montreal or Toronto. It sends out its pay car all over the line, and it takes the company really a month to get the sheets made up, and have the pay car out and back again ready to start the next month. I move that this Bill be sent to the Railway Committee for consideration. While I have every sympathy with the men, I do not think it is right to force a measure such as this through the House at this hour of the night when so few members are present, and when the matter is one which was before the Railway Committee last year.

It is a very poor reason to say that the members are not in the House. If they are not, it is through no fault of mine. I have taken out the clause to which objection was made, and which provides that the companies shall pay back any money they had retained. I have done this because I have been made to understand that it would be impossible for the companies to do otherwise than keep part of the money back. The men will, therefore, have to work four weeks before they can draw two weeks pay, and that will give ample time to the companies to prepare their pay-lists every two weeks. In the old country the railway companies pay every two weeks although they have 65,000 employees at work. In New York also, and in Canada we have some railway companies which pay every two weeks.
What railways in Canada pay every two weeks?
I cannot mention the name, but it is one which was mentioned to me by Senator Casgrain.
It is a short railway line?

If the men are two weeks behind, the company has plenty of time to make up its pay sheets every two weeks; and as to the point that a company's lines extend over a long distance, it takes only four days to get to Vancouver.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This Bill cannot be moved to a final stage to-day, but it can be passed through the committee. I sympathize with the object of the Bill which is that the men should be paid every two weeks if possible; but I would suggest that the third reading should stand over in order that the railway companies may be given a hearing before the measure finally passes.
How can the railway companies be heard, if the Bill is not sent to the Railway Committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They can communicate with my hon. friend, I am sure.

Motion agreed to, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

This clause which will be the whole Bill is amended to read as follows:
Section 259 of the Railway Act is amended by inserting the following as subsection 3 to said section 259.
And that the salary or wages of every person employed in the operation, maintenance or equipment of any railway company to which the parliament of Canada has granted aid by means of subsidy or guarantee, shall be paid not less frequently than once in each two weeks during the terms of his or her employment.
The Minister of Railways ought to be present when this Bill is being considered. Would it apply to the Intercolonial railway, and what views would he have in regard to it?
The Minister of Railways asked me to say that he has seen the amendment to be proposed by my hon. friend and entirely concurs in it and' is quite prepared to support the Bill in itfe amended form.
Then he would think it feasible to pay every two weeks on the Intercolonial?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He approves of the amendment.
- Mr. PERLEY. Have the government consulted the railways in regard to this matter?

The Bill has been before the House a couple of years, and I think the

minister has discussed it fully with the representatives of the railways.

I think the government should take the responsibility for such a Bill and make it a government measure if they decide to pass it, particularly at this hour of the night when it is forced through without discussion.
Would railways to which aid had not been given be affected by this?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That would be my view.
Would this refer to employees on board ships operated by railway companies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think it applies to ships at all.
Bill reported.
